speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Turriff) last evening asked me a question in regard to the pay of colonels. I was out of the House at the time, but I think that, in the interest of the public, I should reply to him. He asked whether or not colonels in Canada were getting $15 to $20 a day, while those at the front were getting only $6. The pay of the officers of the Canadian expeditionary forces is exactly the same in Canada as it is in England or at the front. A lieutenant-colonel gets $5 a day pay and $1.25 field allowance. When he reaches London, and when he is at the front, however, he gets four shillings a day extra. That is the exact position so far as the pay of the Canadian expeditionary forces is concerned, whether in Canada or abroad, with the exception I have mentioned, that if an officer is abroad he gets four shillings a day extra for messing allowance. There is a slight extra pay for officers who are obliged to reside in London because of the extra cost of living in London.

Taxes are usually unwelcome, and we are all more or less willing that our neighbour shall pay his full proportion. I have not yet found a man who is unwilling to pay his full share, but I wish to bring to the attention of the minister some of the conditions connected with this proposed extra imposition. Not a few industries engaged in the manufacture of munitions and other commodities influenced by the war assert that after the war there will be a very critical period of readjustment. Some of them fear that during that period of readjustment they will be able to do nothing more than pay running expenses. The most conservative of these have been preparing for that period by placing to one side each year a reasonable reserve, feeling that when their present large business ceases-as we hope it will very shortly-they. will find themselves, under the new system of taxation, in a serious financial plight. They tell me that during the two or three years succeeding the war these reserves will be used up in their effort to readjust themselves to new conditions and to prepare for a staple business in the future. Some of them, I understand, think that the action of the Government in taking such a large proportion of the amount they now have on hand will cause them to come to a condition of practical bankruptcy during the period of readjustment. I feel confident that the minister, far from having that in mind, would like to protect our industries against this result. To my mind this is the most serious aspect of the matter; the figures that have been presented to me by some concerns lead me to believe that there is a good deal in the contention.
I was struck very forcibly the other night by the remarks of the hon. member for Dauphin. I agree that in order to produce
a revenue in the years to coune, a good many of our former theories will have to go by the board. Methods recognized as proper for the raising of revenue in years gone by will still be used1, but they will have to be supplemented by others. What shall these others be? I think it is the consensus of opinion throughout Canada that these taxes should not be imposed on the producers of agricultural products. In fact, I am strongly of the opinion that we shall have to deal with the tariff from a different angle. The farmer must .be enabled to produce as cheaply and in as large quantities as possible. If his output be restricted, none of the rest of us need look for any great prosperity, because, while industrial development is desirable, it will for a great many years be true of Canada that the basis of our prosperity .must be found in the farms. We shall have to go a long way towards reducing the cost of production and giving the farmer the freest opportunity to sell where he can get the best market and to buy as cheaply as possible all the implements that he uses in production. In a recent trip that I had West, this view was impressed upon me more strongly than ever. Striking instances came to my attention of real hardship to the men who were trying to produce. In the future we shall have to do two things: first, assist the man on the farm so that he can compete with all others the world over who are engaged in the same business; and, second, readjust our tariff with a view to raising as large an amount of money as possible. That, rather than protection, should be the chief object in view. We shall have to go a long way in the scientific arrangement of our tariff in ordbr to raise the greatest amount of money without restricting the ability of the man on the farm to produce. I know the minister will say that it is easy to talk in generalities, but the more we look into the financial situation, the more we are inclined to view it from a different standpoint. The time has arrived when the greatest good to the greatest number .should be the object of the framing of tariffs, and the greatest good will come to the .greatest number only when we enable those engaged in our basic industry, so far as it is possible to do so, unrestrictedly to produce and to sell.
Another remark in that speech which struck me forcibly was in reference to unoccupied lands in the West. I think we are under a kind of delusion as to the amount of good land available for homestead in the West.

1 hear men speaking of the millions and millions of acres of good land remaining available for homesteading, but I believe that the estimate of many men will have to be revised as to the quantity of land still unoccupied. A large quantity of land may yet remain open for homesteading, but there is not so much as people imagine. In the years to come, under new conditions and under new methods, a great deal of this land may be brought under cultivation, but to my mind we have not available for homesteading at the present time such a large quantity of land as some of us think. If it be true, as the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Cruise) said the other night, that there are held in the West' many million acres of land from which no revenue is derived, but the value of which is increasing rapidly on account of the improvement of other lands in the West, then under the new conditions we shall have to devise some scheme of dealing with these lands from a revenue point of view and from the point of view of general development. A large quantity of these lands is exempt from provincial taxation; and if normal conditions existed, I would feel it would perhaps be a dangerous thing to suggest that such lands ought to be taxed, when by agreement they are exempt from taxation; but we are at the present moment in a situation in which every man, woman and child in Canada has to submit to taxation to which neither he nor she ever before expected to have to submit, and we shall all willingly and even gladly offer to pay our share in order that there may be no difficulty from a financial point of view as to Canada being able to do her part in bringing the war to a final and conclusive victory. Those who hold these lands ought to bear their share of the burden, and I believe, whichever party may be in power, it is their duty to ascertain without delay some means whereby this land, which is now very valuable, may contribute its share of taxation for the carrying on of this great struggle in which we are engaged. No hardship will be suffered by anybody if we take part of the profits, or what we call the unearned increment.
Does the hon. member refer to railway lands as well as to lands held by private individuals?

I certainly do; I refer to all lands that are unproductive and that are held for speculative purposes, whether they be owned by railways or by private

individuals. These lands are at present of great value and most of them adjoin railways, whereas a settler coming in ordinarily has to go many miles from a Tailway and at times has to travel over mile after mile of such lands adjoining railways which land he can not secure as a homestead and which he would have to purchase at a very high figure. I know the objections that will be raised, such a violation of agreement and so on; but many years have passed since some of those agreements were made, and we are in a situation now where, while I would not advocate a violation of agreement, I would certainly call in every man interested in these lands and say to him: we propose to devise some means whereby these lands will contribute their share towards the carrying on of this war.
If taxation be imposed on these vacant lands a tendency will be created to dispose of them to men who will cultivate them. If these millions of acres of land in the Great West, now untilled and out of the hands of the Government, were made productive, the railway situation, which is serious, would soon be solved, because in our western country there is a sufficient acreage -to provide for our transportation companies freight which would keep busy, not two railways, but the three transcontinental railways and many more branch lines than we have at present. The railway problem is a serious one and one not easy to solve, but it is worthy of the attention of the Government, and I want to repeat that such taxation would very materially aid our financial situation and would practically solve many of the difficulties that have arisen in connection with our railways, because, while at the present moment we may have in some directions a greater railway mileage than is warranted by the present production of Canada, we have not a greater mileage than is warranted by the developed productiveness of Canada, and if these acres are made productive much of our trouble in connection with the railways would be removed.
There is another point that I wish to urge again upon the attention of the Government. The more I think of it the more I am convinced that there is a source of revenue that we are not touching in this Bill that ought to be touched and touched now, and, if you will allow me, Sir, to say so, touched well. We have in the city of Ottawa and in every other large city in this country men who will not be taxed at all under this Bill, who are not assisting in the employment of men and who are not assisting in the production,

directly at least, of anything connected with this war, while our young men, who, on the farms and in the shops, have been assisting in the productiveness of the country, are at present at the front fighting. The .men who have their money invested in industries are paying liberally and are glad to pay their share into the national coffers for the carrying on of this war, but there are scores of men who have their wealth invested in mortgages and other securities, many of whom are not aiding in the development of any Canadian industry. Some of our wealthiest men have their cash invested in American railway securities and other investments which I could name, and these are not contributing anything, nor will they contribute anything under this measure, and I believe, therefore, that the Government will be justified even now in devising a scheme whereby the wealth of the country, as outlined in the few remarks I have made, will be taxed thoroughly. We speak of conscription of men, but there is another duty whidh the Government ought to undertake, and that is the conscription of wealth, in order that the two may go hand in hand for the carrying on of this great war. The Minister of Finance says rightly that taxation of incomes has been left to the provinces and municipalities. That is true, buit the income tax collected by the municipalities throughout the province of Ontario, for instance, scarcely touches the fringe of what this source of wealth ought to contribute in this time of stress. The province touches this source to a certain extent by adding one mill on the dollar to the assessment throughout Ontario, but that is a mere pittance, and I again urge upon the Government that while nearly all classes are paying taxes, some being taxed very heavily, there is a class that is not touched, and for the duration of the war at least a tax ought to be imposed on this wealth wherever found, and, in particular, a tax ought to be imposed on the incomes of men who have their money invested in mortgages and in securities outside of Canada, on which investments they are taking practically no risk and which are not furnishing employment to a single man, woman or child in this country.
I submit that to the Finance Minister and trust that even at this late stage he will devise some means by which this concentrated wealth that is now untouched may be reached, in order that the burden of taxation may be more evenly distributed among our people. I can assure the minister that I have not met in this Dominion a single
man who is not willing to pay his fair share of taxation in order that we may do our full duty in this war, because as I have said before, and it is worth repeating, if the Allies lose in this war it will in my view not be worth while being a Canadian any longer. We must leave nothing undone, and I again urge that one available source of taxation which should be reached is the incomes of these men of wealth, which under the present taxation are not touched at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Graham) has in a thoughtful speech discussed the question- of the policy of taxation which should be adopted in this country to meet our requirements in connection with the war. The policy of any Government in a situation of this kind must necessarily depend upon the financial situation as it from time to time presents itself. I suppose when this war broke out none of us thought it would last three years. Some of us were of the opinion that it might last one year or perhaps two, but I think no one believed at that time that at the end of three years we should still be looking forward to another year or more of war.
Kitchener said it would last three years.	^

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is so, but I think that few in this country, and I know that few in England, believed that the war would last for so long a period.
My hen. friend has raised the question of the policy of taxation which should he pursued in connection with the financing of the war. There are two principles which I have endeavoured to follow in the finan- * cial administration of the country. In the first place I have thought it advisable to make long-date loans in order that the country during the progress of the war or in the possibly trying period following the conclusion of the war might not be hampered or embarrassed by short-date maturities falling due. I think that is a sound principle, and that we have been wise in adopting it. The second principle which I have adopted is this: that we should so aim by increasing our revenues and diminishing our expenditures for purposes other than war, to be able during each year to meet not only all current expenditure, including the interest on a rapidly increasing war indebtedness and a large expenditure for pensions, but at the same time be able to pay a substantial portion of the principal of our war expenditure. It strikes me that

those are very sound principles in connection with the financial administration of the country in time of war.
I pointed out in the Budget speech that we had been able out of the revenues of the past year, which had been derived from the various modes of taxation which we have adopted, to pay not only all current and all capital expenditure-and in current expenditure I am including the increased interest amounting to some $20,000,000, on our increased national debt due to the war-Ibut also to pay all pensions and at the same time devote $60,000,000 to the payment of the principal of our war ex' penditure. Now, if we can succeed in doing that, the war expenditure of the Dominion during the war would not be a formidable problem for the Dominion to face, and in that connection we must bear in mind that our expenditures for war are rapidly increasing, that they will be greater for the year 1917 than they were for the year 1916, and that they will he greater for the year 1918 than for the year 1917. I tried to make a perfectly frank statement to the House in my Budget speech. I said we could look forward at the end of next year to a national debt of $1,200,000,000-I think that is an outside figure, rather than attempt to minimize the seriousness of the burden which would be imposed upon us, and which I know we are all glad to bear in connection with the war.
The policy of any Government in war time as to taxation must depend upon the financial situation as it presents itself from time to time. It has appeared to us that the measure of taxation which we have brought down in this Budget is reasonably adequate to cope with the situation as it presents itself at the present time. I said during the debate that it was possible and even probable that we might have to resort to a measure of income taxation as the war developed and our financial requirements became greater. I also stated that we might have to consider, and I repeat it to-day, other sources of taxation different from those which we have adopted up to date. My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) in his very thoughtful speech has put forward different methods of taxation, some of which he appears to favour, and all of which he desires the House to consider. In his closing remarks he referred especially to income taxation. Now, I have given this matter of income taxation my most careful consideration, and I have reached the conclusion, which I believe is sound, that at present it is not advisable TSir Thomas White.]
to impose an income taxation. I hope the House will pardon me if I develop briefly some of the arguments which have led me to that conclusion; most of which were touched upon in the Budget speech.
Many statements have been made in this House by hon. gentlemen who have not had the opportunity of going into this matter as a Finance Minister is able to go into it, indicating an opinion upon their part that very large sums indeed would be raised by an income taxation measure. For instance, the hon. member for Dauphin, in the course of his speech stated that we should raise $50,000,000 from income taxation. I doubt very much if the hon. member has gone into the matter statistically to see whether any such sum could be realized by income taxation. I have no hesitation in saying myself that no such sum could be realized in this country by a measure of income taxation. You might ask me on what I ground that view. Well, in the United States, for instance, which has 12 or 13 times the population of Canada-and at least 25, and I should not be surprised if it were 40 of 50 times our wealth-they have had income taxation for some years. It is a pretty heavy tax, being 2 per cent upon incomes from $3,000 upwards. As soon as the income reaches $20,000 there is an increase of one per cent; when it reaches $40,000 there is an increase of two per cent, and so on upon a graduated scale running up to thirteen per cent on an income of $2,000,000. That is a fairly heavy income tax.

What is the initial rate?
#

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Twenty mills on the dollar or two per cent, which is about the Tate of municipal taxation in Toronto and most of the other cities in Canada. This tax has been in effect in the United States for some years, and consequently the machinery for collecting it-a very important matter has been perfected. Yet, the amount realized from this tax, which is imposed not only upon individuals but upon corporations in respect of their net profits, was, for the year 1915, only $80,000,000, and for the year 1916, $124,000,000. The population of the United1 States is twelve or thirteen times that of Canada, and the wealth of the United States is at least twenty-five times that of Canada, I believe. This matter has been gone into by my department, and we are familiar witli the income tax assessments in the neighbouring republic; and the conclusion- we have reached is that on the scale of income

taxation in force in the United States today the Dominion of Canada could not hope to raise more than $5,000,000 or $6,000,000.
Do I understand that the man in the United States with an income of $2,000,000 pays two per cent-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
First, he pays
two per cent, and. then an additional thirteen per cent.

That is fifteen per cent
on $2,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is as I understand it. So this income tax proposition is one to raise in the Dominion of Canada not more at the outside than $7,000,000 or $8,000,000.

It is admitted, I believe, that there is greater wealth in the United States than in Great Britain. Why, then, cannot they in the United States collect as much by income tax as is collected by that method in Great Britain? Or why could not we collect as much in proportion to our wealth as Great Britain collects in proportion to hers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have to consider first whether the wealth is concentrated or not. I think we do not realize the enormous amount of concentrated wealth in Great Britain. Well, suppose we should raise $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 by an income tax beginning at two per cent and running up to fifteen per cent-a very heavy tax-or even suppose we managed to increase it and to raise $10,000,000 or $12,000,000, we should even then have slightly less than the amount raised by the excess profits tax in the first year of its operation, which was the least productive year of all. In the first year of that tax we raised $12,500,000; and, as I pointed out in my Budget speech, we expect to raise more the second year, because the second year was on an increased business. So, I ask the House, when considering income taxation in the Dominion of Canada, to have regard to the comparatively small amount-that is small in terms of Dominion finance-that could be raised by this means. Reference has been made to certajn gentlemen in Ottawa, Toronto, Montreal, and other large cities-
On several occasions the Minister of Finance has said that the cost of collecting an income fax would be very large?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Has the hon. minister made calculations on that subject? Could he tell us about what it will cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am glad my hon. friend called that to my attention, because I had intended to speak of it. It is not possible to make an estimate as to the cost, but I can say without hesitation that it would be very large in proportion to the amount of revenue that the tax would realize.
Has the hon. minister any figures showing the cost in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I could get that, but I have not it here. This is one of the points that has been raised, and I want to deal with it fairly, and, I hope, in such a way as to afford information which will be available for members in reaching a conclusion. One difficulty in applying a federal income tax in Canada arises from the fact that we have a sparse population scattered over a territory at least as large as Europe. What does that mean? It means that we should have to cover the whole country, geographically speaking, in order to make sure that we were actually assessing the tax on all incomes down to $3,000, or $2,000, or whatever the limit of exemption might be. We should have to have a Civil 'Service, for that is what it would amount to, over the length and breadth of this country. We should have to cover every municipality, rural as well as urban, because in any towilship there might be one or more men with incomes greater than the limit of exemption. I do not mean to say that because the administration would be difficult that this tax should not be resorted 'to at all. But I do say that one test of the advisability of a tax is that the percentage cost of collection should be low. That is an axiom of taxation. But it is easy to see that in this case the cost of collection would be high. All that I say now is subject to this, which I have said before and now repeat: we may find it necessary to resort to an income tax, and if we find it necessary, for my part, I will not hesitate to resort to it.
Reference has been made to gentlemen in Ottawa, Toronto, Montreal, and other cities, who derive large incomes from interest upon mortgages or other sources, and who are exempt from taxation. It must be borne in mind that any tax in the Dominion must be general in character. I cannot bring in a Bill to tax A, or B, or C; the measure must apply to the citizens of
Commons
the country generally, commencing, oi course, at a certain minimum of income, and graduated to the highest income that is derived in Canada. I cannot bring in a Bill to tax a few wealthy men.
Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well because, for one reason, the cost of administration would probably eat up the amount realized.
That is not a reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) says that is not an answer. Well, I think it is, and we will let it go at that. He will object to anything I say, no matter what, so I hope he will not mind if I simply meet his assertion with counter-assertion.
Don't get mad.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, certainly not with my hon. friend from Pictou. There is another phase of this matter. People in Canada to-day are giving very large sums to the Canadian Patriotic Fund, to the Red Cross Fund, and to other funds in connection with the war. The people, rich and poor, have been most generous in regard to tnese funds. My own opinion is that if a stiff income tax were added to the other burdens of the war it might result in a considerable dimunition in the amount subscribed to the Patriotic, Red Cross, and other funds. I do not put that forward as a conclusive reason why an income tax should not be adopted, but I do say that when we consider the expediency of an income taxation measure, it is wise to consider how much is being contributed voluntarily by the people, irrespective of class or rank, to the patriotic funds. That is all I purpose saying at the present time upon the question of an income tax.
My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has spoken of the tariff. I shall not deal with that at any length in answer to my hon. friend because the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has given notice of an amendment which he proposes to move on the second reading of the taxation proposals, and I think I shall reserve what I have to say on that head until that amendment is under discussion. But, I should like to say this to my hon. friend from South Renfrew in regard to the tariff, and I am sure the information -will be of interest to the House, that the measures which we have adopted in regard to the
TSir Thomas White.]
tariff have been fruitful to the utmost extent of our expectations. I shall quote just three figures. The House will recall that we increased the tariff by 71 per cent and 5 in the year 1915. Since then the revenue of the Dominion from customs duties has been as follows:
1915		 $ 79,000,000
1916	 103,000,000.
1917	 147,000,000
There was an increase in 1916 over 1915 of $24,000,000 and an increase in 1917 over 1916 of $44,000,000. You must not forget, in considering this question of taxation, that the very backbone of the revenues of the Dominion is and is bound to be the tariff. We must look to the tariff to produce a very large amount indeed in order to meet the requirements of the Dominion for this war and other expenditures. I have a calculation as to the amount derived by the Dominion Government in respect to the 71 and 5 per cent increases made in 1915.
Does my hon. friend distinguish between the 71 per cent on free goods and the 71 per cent On dutiable goods?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is on both. In 1916, under the 5 per cent and the 71 per cent increases, we derived $25,000,000 from the customs duties war tax and in 1917 we derived $37,000,000 from the same taxation.
Is that from the tariff on free goods as well as the other?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On both, because we impose 71 per cent and 5 per cent on all goods.
I understand that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is on both.

Will the minister state now what proportion of the $37,000,000 of revenue received from the 71 per cent surtax came from free goods, or goods which were formerly free, and what proportion from goods which were dutiable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
From free goods,

Mr. A* K. MACLEAN: And $17,000,000 from dutiable goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That would follow -$17,000,000 on dutiable goods. But the point I am making is that the increase in the tariff has produced very substantial sums towards the expenditures of the Dominion for war and other purposes.

The hon. member for South Renfrew referred to the business tax that is now before the House .for consideration. He stated that after -the war there would be a period of readjustment and that he shared the apprehension of some business men and friends that this taxation, by reason of it being so expensive, would cause them a great deal of embarrassment and 4 p.m. even might force some of them into bankruptcy. I hardly see how that result could occur. In the first place, there have been three years since the outbreak of the war that the business profits war tax has been applied. In the first place, as I have stated, we realized $12,500,000, notwithstanding that there was a good deal of dislocation of business in that first period. In the second year I should be surprised if we should not realize $20,000,000 or more. The third year will probably be the best of all. It would have been the best of all if we had allowed the taxation which was introduced last year to stand, hut we are increasing that taxation by the provisions of the measure now before the committee, and, therefore, the amount which will be realized from excess profits on business in this country for the last accounting period of the three years will he very large; 'how large I am not prepared to say, because I have not the figures touching this estimate.
On what does my hon. friend place that estimate of increased revenue? Is it on the prospect of increased business, or increased prices, or both?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As the taxation is levied in respect of profits, it would be in respect of increased business, but I suppose you could hardly consider business without considering prices in Connection with it.
If you had the same business with increased prices it would be to the disadvantage of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not quite understand the hon. gentleman's point.

If the manufacturers
were increasing their prices and if by reason of increased prices they have increased profits, it would not be a very satisfactory condition, because the consumer would have to pay those profits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Abnormal profits are being obtained by many businesses in Canada to-day. I have no doubt they are taking substantially as much as the market will afford them. Their profits are abnormal. What the Government are doing is
this: They are saying to them: Your profits are, say, 20, or 30, or 40 per cent; we propose to step in and take a certain amount of those profits, because we regard them as abnormal; they are greater than you would have made had there been no war. Let us see what the extent of this tax is. The measure is limited to three years. I stated last year that it would be limited to three years, and I state so to-day. For the first two years we allow a company 7 per cent and an individual 10 per cent profit. We say to them: We shall not touch your profits up to 7 per cent, or 10 per cent, hut if you make 15 per cent we will take 2 per cent away from you. I am only using the amount of 15 per cent by way of illustration. I shall deal with an incorporated company rather than an individual in giving my illustration. We say to an incorporated company: If you obtain profits of 15 per cent we will leave you 13 and take 2. Under this new measure which we are now proposing we say to them that we will take 2 per cent up to 15 per cent and half of the amount which they make between 15 and 20 per cent, and if they make over 20 per cent we shall take three-quarters of the whole.
I admit that it is a Dretty stiff tax, it is a heavy tax. But I would ask the House to hear in mind (because the tax has been criticised on account of its severity) that capital as defined in the Business Profits War Tax Act includes reserve and undistributed profits, I do not myself believe that the ordinary commercial company has any very serious ground of complaint.
Are borrowings treated as capital?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. As I said, I do not believe that the ordinary commercial company has any serious ground of complaint if, when it is earning 15 per cent upon capital and reserve, we say: We will allow you 13 per cent and tax 2 per cent; or if they make the additional 5 per cent we say that we will take one-half, or if they make over 20 per cent we .say we will take three-quarters of the excess amount. It is a fact that there are concerns in. this country that have been making 50 per cent, 75 per cent or 100 per cent in the way of profits in the last year, and this taxation is without question severe upon those firms and companies. There is no doubt about that. I pointed out the other day that this question had more than a business aspect, and although I was misunderstood, I was not indulging in rhetoric. I used the argu-

inent because I believed it had a real bearing upon this question of taxation. I stated that the people of this country were bearing great hardships, and making great sacrifices, owing to the war. I said that men were interrupting their employment, giving up their vocations and going to the war; that parents were sending their sons forward; and I said that I thought it was proper under those circumstances that, in the event of excessive profits having been earned owing to the war, a very substantial part of those profits should be taken for the State. I asked the House to believe and I, at all events, believe that it is a relevant argument. I think it is strengthened by the announcement of the Prime Minister the other day that it is proposed to introduce compulsory service into Canada. We must bear in mind that in the event of firms in this country getting abnormal profits, 30 per cent, 40 per cent, 50 per cent, 60 per cent or 100 per cent, the sentiment of the public is apt to be offended, and in that way our effort in the war likely to be diminished, if excess profits so great as that are permitted to private enterprise at a time when these sacrifices are being made by the people. I am the first to say in that connection that the men who have made these profits: have made them under conditions that exist in thi6 country, and that they are just as patriotic as the rest of us. They are among the leading citizens of Canada; they, too, have sent their sons forward and still continue to do everything they can to assist in the war. But the fact remains that very large profits have been made, and, so far as I am concerned, I have been unable to see that the Government would be justified in allowing those abnormal profits to be made without stepping in and taking a substantial part for the State. In other words, I believe that that argument, which might be criticised as a sentimental argument, is a real argument, having regard to the fact that we are carrying on this war and calling upon the people to make sacrifices of every kind in connection with it.
The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has, as I said, expressed some apprehension lest the tax might be unduly heavy and force some of these firms into bankruptcy. Considering that we have taken only one-quarter of the excess profits in excess of 7 per cent during the years 1915 and 1916, and considering that this increased taxation applies only to the last accounting term of the three year period, I
[Sir Thomas White.1
am of opinion that his apprehensions are not well founded, 'because most of the firms that made large profits last year made much larger profits in the previous year, and many of them made large profits in the year preceding that, which was a period of considerable dislocation of business. As the hon. member for South Renfrew said, we are on common ground in desiring that nothing should be done that would injure the industries of this country; but I am of the view that no such untoward consequences as he apprehends are likely to ensue.

The minister will remember that, some days ago, he was good enough to tell me that he would be willing to submit a statement of the excess profits of the flour milling companies of last year, from which the tax was taken. I should like very much to have them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I stated last year when this matter was under consideration by the House that should returns be called for by the House we should, of course, be glad to bring them down. These returns deal with the private business of individuals and companies throughout Canada. If any member desires information respecting the assessments levied against them, I would suggest that he give his notice on the Order Paper, and it will then be for the House to determine whether, in any particular case, those returns should be brought down. I have no objection personally to bringing them down; I am in the hands of the House. But I think if any hon. member desires information as to the assessment against an industry or an individual firm in an industry, he should move for it in the usual way in the House, and it would then be for the House to discuss the matter and determine whether -they should be brought down or not.
I am sorry the minister did not say that. I think the minister said that if any member of the House desired the returns they would be brought down.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can quote
almost my exact words. I stated to my hon. friend that if the House, as I said last year, adopted a resolution, the returns would be brought down.

The minister did not
say that the other day.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What would be the advice of my hon. friend to the House when this motion was made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot say in advance what my view would be except this, that if it developed that the House desired or the majority of the House desired information as to any particular assessment, or all assessments so far as I am concerned, the House would be entitled to the information because the House having imposed the taxation is entitled to know the result.
That is the majority of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would not say that. I reserve to myself the right to consider what the motion is. If it were aimed at an individual and for some purpose that I considered other than the public interest,
I might give my expression of opinion that while I would be very glad to give to any particular member the information personally, I would hesitate to make it public.

I will tell the minister what I wanted. I think I explained my own view as being that the people of Canada and this Parliament have a right to know what are the excess 'profits of every manufacturer engaged in producing foodstuffs, such as flour, or other necessaries of life, the price of which has gone up to an inordinate extent, beyond all reason, and that the public have a right to know what are the excess profits out of which the Government is getting its share.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend desires information along that line, I suggest that he move for it in the House and we will consider what action will be taken.
I will say further that it was agreed last year on the part of almost every member of the House, that information of this character, which touched the business of individual firms and companies throughout the country, should not be made public unless called for by the House. If my hon. friend desires information 'concerning the assessment of any person. industry or group of industries, he shall have it. If any member of the House desired to know in a confidential way, for his own information, what the assessment of any individual was, I should feel that I would give it to him.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
When my hon/ friend says that he is in the hands of the House in regard to this matter, I think that he evades the question- The House does not give guidance to him; it rather expects guidance from him. I should not say that
hi? advice would be followed in every case, but certainly the Hpuse would not pass in judgment upon a matter of this kind until it had the advice of my hon. friend. A motion made with a view to inquisitiveness or with a desire to inquire into the business of any individual should not, perhaps, be granted without cause shown. No pne desires to have specific information concerning the business of Mr. So-and-So. I make no -insinuation, but it is conceivable that one firm may have obtained advantage at the expense of another, and if information is asked for in that connection, I think my hon. friend will agree that the public have a right to information concerning certain businesses of a general character, such as railways and shipping companies. The flour business is of such a character that I think the information referred to shpuld be given to the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think I may substantially agree with what my right hon. friend has said, but it is unusual to ask a minister in advance what attitude he will take with regard to a motion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We have understood ever since this matter came up in the House last session that this information wpuld be given without any question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will take opportunity during the course of this discussion to place before the committee what I did say last year. My recollection of what I said is that if the House desired information respecting- these assessments, it was only reasonable, having regard to the fact that the House had authorized the taxation, that the information should be given. I do. not desire to withhold any information from the House at any time, but I cannot state in advance what action I shall take with regard to any motion which may be put on the Order Paper. I shall have to consider the motion on its merits, and the arguments adduced in support of it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That means that the House is not entitled to the information unless it is moved for.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend himself said a few moments ago that a request for information for merely inquisitorial purposes -should not be granted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Exactly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend says that if a motion asking for information is put forward for inquisitorial



reasons, it should be opposed, but if put forward with the bona fide intention of obtaining information in the public interest, it should be granted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I understood from the discussion which took place last year that the details of the receipts in respect of this taxation would be given. No one expects that the details of every particular assessment will be given. It is not expected that we should have a return showing that Mr. So-and-So paid $500, and somebody else $600; but we do think that we should have information as to the amounts paid into the treasury by different classes of industries. I think that information concerning industries of the character to which reference has just been made [DOT] should be given without motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my right hon. friend will place on the Order Paper a resolution asking for returns with regard to taxation, I shall have no disposition to withhold any information, because I do not believe that my right hon. friend would bring forward a motion of that kind with any other than a proper intention.
I hope the minister does not suppose that I would do anything of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not for a moment. The hon, gentleman is the- last person I would think of in that re'gard.

A few days ago, when
this matter was under consideration, I suggested that the committee was entitled to this information, especially with regard to the flour and the milling industries. I understood the minister to say then that he would bring down the information. If the minister is not prepared to do that, I think he ought to allow the consideration of this resolution to stand until the information is obtained. It is not mere inquisitiveness which prompts members of this Committee to seek information as to the excess profits, running all the way from 20 to 100 per cent, which the manufacturers of flour and the producers of other necessaries of life are obtaining, a portion of which goes into the treasury, and about which the minister boasts so enthusiastically every time he refers to his Budget. The country has a right to know what these enormous excessive profits are which are taken out of the people and what portion of them has gone into the treasury.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As to what I
stated the other day, I quote from, page 1511 of Hansard:
Mr. Pugsley: Could the minister not furnish to the House a statement of the excess profits which have been made by one industry as an example? Take the flour milling industries of the country.
Sir Thomas White:	I could give them if
they were asked for. As I said last year, if a motion is adopted in the House for returns of the assessment of this business tax, the papers will be laid on the Table.
Read a little further.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is the
answer that 1 made.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Read a little further.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I stated the other day that if a motion were adopted, we should be prepared to bring down the papers.

If my hoe. friend will
read a little further, he will find that, whether he intended to or not, he led us to believe that no formal motion would be necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think
I could have stated it more clearly than I did; that if the House adopted a motion, I would bring the papers down. In the discussion of this matter last year I said, as reported on page 2637 of Hansard:
I do not think it desirable that publicity should be given in the way that my hon. friend suggests. I have already said that, if Parliament desires a return, such a return shall be brought down. This is a business tax dealing with private affairs of individuals, firms, and companies, engaged in business throughout the country, and while Parliament is entitled to any information as to the results of the tax, I do not believe the details should be advertised any more than is necessary.
That is what I said last year, and I stand by that.

When this matter was discussed a few days ago, the member for Carleton, N.B., (Mr. Carvell) said:
The big milling companies publish their statements and the companies have a good idea of their profits. But there are hundreds, and I trust thousands of small milling companies and millers all over Canada, and I think the public have a right to know how much they are contributing and how this tax has been levied. That information should be brought down, I think, without Parliament demanding it.
To which the minister replied:
That was discussed last year in the House, and I then made the same statement that I have made to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What was the
statement that I made to-day? It was that if a resolution was adopted, the papers would be brought down,
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have just read what I said.

Mr. Carvell said:-
Mr. Carvell:	Would there he any objection
to producing statements showing the persons, firms and companies, and the amount paid by them for the first accounting period?
Sir Thomas White:	I would consider that.
I do not know whether we have that information. We received some very large cheques in payment of these taxes.
There is no suggestion there of a formal demand. I said a little later on:-
Mr. Pugsley:	The reason I suggested the
milling industry is because the people are intensely interested in the increasing price of flour, and I think that before we pass the Bill we ought to have a statement from the minister of the excess profits of the milling industry last year. I think the public would like to have that.
Sir Thomas White:	That matter can be
raised at any time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree entirely with what I said. If my hon. friend desires any information as to this let him put a question on the Order Paper asking for the information and the matter will receive consideration.
Now is the time, and I may say to the minister that I am asking for the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am asking that the question be put formally.
With all deference to the minister, I say that I think the committee ought-to have the information before coming to a decision in regard to this resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend has just stated that the object of this tax is to obtain a certain definite proportion of the profits in excess of seven per cent. That is a sufficient answer so far as it goes, but there ds another aspect of the case. The complaint has been raised that certain industries are making undue profits; that they are profiting on the needs of the community, profiting and speculating upon the hunger of the people. That complaint has been asserted and it has been denied, but we have the evidence of its correctness. No one supposes that my hon. friend did not properly discharge his duty; that he did not collect all that was due, but he might furnish the public with information for which they are seeking and which might be of value at the present time in reducing the high cost of bread and other food.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon.
friend is quite fair in his presentation of his views. He says that this information might be of use at the present time when the price of food is high, but that matter is entirely separable from what we are doing now in considering a taxation principle.

How is it separable?
SiT THOMAS WHITE: If my hon. friend will put on the Order Paper a question asking for the information he desires, that matter will be considered on its merits, just as this matter is being considered on its merits; but to say:	Will the minister
bring down the information regarding the amount of taxation imposed upon members of a particular industry, and then when the matter comes up again, to ask for similar particulars in connection with another industry, is not a proper method of dealing with this measure, because the two matters are separable. My right hon. friend is quite correct in saying that the people are interested in the profits of these companies from the standpoint of the high cost of food. If he will move on that ground, personally I should be prepared to give quite favourable consideration to his motion, but the matter does not necessarily arise in connection with the consideration of this measure, and therefore, I cannot concur in the suggestion that we should defer consideration of this measure until that and .other information is brought down, because I do not believe it is cognate to this measure.

It was stated officially about six weeks ago that there were still 102,000,000 bushels of wheat in Canada, and since that time the price of wheat has advanced by one. dollar a bushel, which would mean an advance of $102,000,000. We know that the Minister of Agriculture was compelled to go to an outside purchasing commission to secure wheat for seed and that the price, was fixed at fifty cents a bushel over the price in effect six weeks ago. Will this purchasing commission contribute of its excess profits under the Business Profits War Tax Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not understand the question of my hon. friend at all. I know nothing about the purchasing commission he speaks of. The Act is very simple in its application; if any firm engaged in business makes profits beyond a certain percentage, then the tax would apply. I am sorry that I can not answer my hon. friend's question, because I do not understand it.
We are told that the Allied Purchasing Commission controls all the wheat in Canada to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the British Government.
Yes, and Canada through her official representative had to go to this commission to obtain the wheat required for seed purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that.

And the price was fixed at fifty cents per bushel over the price in effect six weeks ago. It is apparent, therefore, that some persons have made $50,000,000 on this deal if the price remains at that level until they get rid of that wheat. Will they contribute under the excess profits tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not understand the question of my hon. friend, because in the first place I do not know that the Minister of Agriculture did go to the British commission, although he may have gone; nor do I know that he got the wheat and paid for it.. I would be glad to answer my hon. friend's question if I had the information.
The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) referred to the question of conscription of wealth. That is a rather vague term, and I could not help but reflect that his remarks were somewhat inconsistent.
(Sir Thomas White.]
He started out by attacking this tax-and I must say that his criticism was of a moderate and fair character-as being too severe, and then he suggested that the time had come for conscription of wealth. Without using that term, the Government in connection with this excess profits measure, now before the House, is endeavouring to take a substantial portion of profits which might be regarded as abnormal and arising largely from war conditions. That is one of the principles underlying this new taxation.

With regard to the statement of the minister that he does not think the question of profits, which the milling companies and companies producing other necessaries of life have made, and out of which profits the Government has derived in the past year and expects to derive in the present year large sums, has anything to do with the resolution now before the committee, I respectfully beg to differ from my hon. friend; I think it has a great deal to do with it. The minister has stated that out of these taxes he expects to derive a certain amount of revenue for the purpose of carrying on the services of the country. In that connection, Parliament surely has a right to know as to whether that expected revenue is to be derived from enormously excessive profits or whether it is to be derived from reasonably excessive profits. This Parliament and this country have a right to know that; we have a right to know whether those excess profits out of which the minister expects to derive a proportion *of his revenue, are 50 or 100 or 200 per cent beyond what are fair and reasonable profits. I am surprised that the minister should ask a committee to pass a resolution and at the same time refuse to furnish us with that reasonable information which we have a right to expect. I certainly understood the minister to state a few days ago that if any hon. member asked for this information. it would be brought down.
Now is the time to bring it down before this resolution is further considered by the committee. My views will not be potent with the minister, of course, if he has determined not to bring the information down, but I think the committee ought not to be asked to pass the resolution until we have that information. This is a question in which the people of this country are taking a most vital interest. The poor people of this Dominion are simply being ground to the dust by the high cost of liv-

ing. Think of it, Mr. Chairman! In this country, which is capable of producing not only two or three or five hundred million bushels of wheat, but thousands of millions of bushels, the price of wheat to-day is $3.30 per bushel, and flour has reached the enormous sum of $16 a barrel. It is simply astounding. And yet the Minister of Finance says he will not tell the House what are the excess profits of the flour millers and other producers of necessaries of life. He wants us to put this resolution through in the dark, without any information at all. Surely it is of interest to this Parliament and to the people of this country to know the amount of these excess profits from which the Minister of Finance proposes to take his share and put it into the treasury. I think it is of vital importance that we should know whether these excess profits are such as might reasonably be expected to be made under war conditions, or whether they are exorbitant profits which this Parliament should not recognize at all, and against which we should take effectual steps in order to relieve the conditions from which the people ,of this country are suffering at the present time. Does not the minister think this a reasonable request? Does he not think he should tell us whether the excess profits of the millers last year were $100,000,000 or $200,000,000 or $300,000,000, so that we might know what his percentage was, because the minister is a partner with the millers in the business of boosting the prices. He has made himself a partner with them, and he has taken no steps since the beginning of the war to keep down the prices. From every million dollars of excess profits which the millers take from the consumers of this country the Minister of Finance takes his share and pute it in the Treasury, and, so far as this House and the country knows, neither he nor his colleagues, not even the Minister of Labour, has ever taken one effectual step to keep prices1 within reasonable limits. The Finance Minister has simply winked at the taking of these excess profits out of the people, and now he comes down to Parliament and asks us to authorize him to take a larger share of these excess profits without giving us the slightest information as to whether these profits are enormous, or simply such as might reasonably be expected under the conditions existing to-day. The minister should not treat this Parliament as a machine to do his bidding. It is not fair to the gentlemen who- sit behind
him. He ought to realize that they have judgment, as they undoubtedly have; he ought to realize that they are men of large intelligence, as they are, but he doee not realize this. He treats them as automatons to do his bidding, and gives them not the slightest information upon which they can act intelligently with regard to the proposal now before the committee. If I had the- power, I would not let the minister go one step further with this resolution until he had given the committee that information.

I desire to support
what my hon. friend from St. John has said as to the importance of furnishing this House and the country with this information, which certainly is as ordinary a piece of information as the House could ever seek from a minister. A certain measure of taxation ie proposed, and yet the Minister of Finance practicaly declines to give the House and the country the names of the men who have made these excess profits and the amounts. My hon. friend suggests there may be some reason why that information should not be given. For myself, I cannot conceive o.f any such reason. The Minister of Finance, however, asks Parliament to authorize him to increase the taxation along these lines, because he says it is the best method of taxation at the present time to raise money to carry on the war. If excess profits have been made, as the Finance Minister says, why should he decline to give the House the information asked for by my hon. friend?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not declining to give the information. If my hon. friend will move for the information, we will consider his motion. My hon. friend has not yet told us what he wants, whether he wants the assessment of "A" or "B" or "C."

The whole of it. The minister should lay on the Table, as every other minister does, a statement of his receipts and expenditures. Why should he not publish a bluebook showing just who are paying these excess profits and the amounts? My hon. friend by innuendo suggests that possibly some business may be injured by giving this information, but this legislation will certainly injure them to a far greater degree if they are making excess profits. Either this additional tax is warranted by some information which the minister has in his possession, and which he has not yet given to the country,

or he has no reason whatever for imposing it. It is certainly not the gentlemen whom the minister proposes to tax that are asking that this information be withheld from the country, because the trade and financial papers throughout the Dominion are simply full of wild denunciations of the Finance Minister for proposing this additional taxation. Their position is that the House ought to know what the facts are, so that the country can see that the Minister of Finance is wrong in proposing this taxation. If this question involved some matter of state policy, or some interest vital to the war would be affected by giving this information, I could well understand the minister following ' the unwritten rule that its publication would not be in the public interest. But as my hon. friend from St. John has so ably pointed out, if there is one thing that strikes at the home of the plain people of this country to-day it is the enormous price which they (have to pay for the right to live. That problem is at the door of every one, but this Government absolutely refuses to deal with the matter in any way. During the time this House has been sitting this session the price of flour has doubled in this country, and so has every other necessary of life. The minister tells this House that there are certain classes in this country who are making excess profits, and he is going to impose additional taxation upon them. The hon. member for St. John argues that if that is the case, the House should be told just who are making excess profits, and what those profits are, because the Minister of Finance is a partner with them in taking this money out of the pockets of the people. We should have that information so that we can tell whether it is wise and practical to extend this taxation on thiB particular class. I think the Finance Minister should give the House without any reservation the amounts he has received from this excess profits tax, and from whom, and then the House will be able to decide whether it is Tight to extend this particular taxation-. I must confess that I was under the impression that my hon. friend would have asked this House to accept ,an amendment to this resolution, but apparently he is going to go on with it regardless of the representations that have been made.
Sir THOtMAS WHITE: I do not quits understsfnd my hon. friend's allusion to an amendment. My hon. friend says that I should have considered an amendment.
fMr. Macdonald.]

I said that I was
under the impression that my hon. friend would have proposed an amendment to the resolution in view of the representations that have been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Along what lines?

Along lines that will readily occur to my hon. friend. Apparently, it has not occurred to him to propose it. When we point out to him that he is taxing industry, and to that extend checking the demand for labour as well as checking production of articles so essential to the country's welfare, that he is preventing capital from doing all that it might do for the development of the country, and ask why he does not tax accumulated wealth, he gives statements which, I submit, are not adequate reasons for the course he is pursuing. He declines to tax the accumulations of the wealthy men of this country who now escape taxation, who pay nothing to the war except an occasional subscription to the Patriotic Fund.
The fiscal argument of the Minister of Finance in the past has been that we cannot impose an income tax because incomes are the special subject of taxation for both municipal and provincial purposes. Sometime in the dim and distant future we may tax incomes, but in the meantime we cannot do so because the provinces and the municipalities impose these taxes. But he taxes corporations and firms, forsooth, and contends that this is the right way for him to raise revenues. I think he has forgotten that the capital invested in these corporations or firms pays provincial taxes and municipal taxes, just as accumulated wealth pays in the form of an income tax. The hon. minister has departed from the sound principles of taxation in dealing with this whole question. Instead of dealing with the matter so that all classes may be made to pay, he is putting off the evil day. He does not follow the example of Gladstone who, when Chancellor of the Exchequer, declared for the sound policy that Britain should pay as much as possible towards the expenses of the war while the war was going on. On the contrary he practically says:	We will pay as little as possible
while the war is going on, we will collect from capital invested in industry, but we will not touch accumulated wealth; we are going to leave to posterity the task of paying for this war. There has arisen in Canada, by reason of the demand that has come for many industrial products, a prosperity under which wealth is made and the

accumulations of wealth increased. Yet the minister touches only the fringe of taxation, he takes from only one class, and leaves the payment for the war to the future, when the time of reaction comes, when we shall need people to come into this country and develop it, when they will probably be frightened away because of the taxes which it will be necessary to impose at that time. I say that is a wrong policy. The 'minister should be preparing now so that we at this time should all be doing our part, when accumulated wealth especially should be doing its part.
The hon. gentleman tells us that it will cost so much to tax these people with accumulated wealth. Why, he has in his own department machinery that is ample to reach the wealthy men of the country who are investing in his loans in order to escape taxation upon their accumulations. With this organization he has been able to reach firms and corporations from the Atlantic to the Pacific and to collect from them his business tax, and with no greater expense he could meet accumulated wealth in such a way that it will be made to pay its proportion toward the public revenue. He knows that a question of this kind is not settled by simply speaking of the cost. He could fix an amount of income beyond which taxes should be imposed in the most stringent way. This tax ought to be imposed, because, in this war time, when everything is at shake, when everything is in the melting-pot, there is no person who should escape the responsibility of contributing, to the extent of his wealth, toward our needs in this war. Our friends in the United States have not hesitated to strike in the most emphatic way at this class of wealth, and by the methods they have adopted they are raising enormous sums. But the hon. minister prefers to leave the burden to posterity. Nor does he give the House the information which would enable hon. members to form a fair judgment on the question, but he simply imposes a tax on business the result of which, according to those best informed on the subject,- is to prevent the extension of industry in Canada.
The minister should be reminded that, before he taxes at all, he should economize, so as to put himself in a better position to provide more money against the expenses of the war. For instance, in public works, we have spent, since 1914, including capital account and consolidated fund account, no less than $47,000,000-practically fifty millions of dollars. Imagine, Mr. Chairman, our making so huge an expenditure in this
war time. Even last year, according to figures given me from Hansard, no less than $15,000,000 was spent on public works. Why should such an expenditure go on and we leave it to posterity to pay these war bills? Why should the minister imperil the future of the country by failure to economize and by these vast expenditures? Consider how expenditures have increased within the last five yeaTS. In Dominion lands last year we spent about $1,500,000 more than we spent in the same service five years ago.
Is there anybody in this country who supposes that there is immigration cpming into Canada which would warrant or justify in any way an expenditure of $1,500,000? So one goes through the various departments. In the Immigration Branch of the Department of the Interior there was an expenditure of $300,000 more than there was four years ago. Why should such extravagance exist? My hon. friend the Minister of Finance talks to the people of Canada about making sacrifices and says that this tax is justifiable because we are sacrificing our men and boys on the battlefield and that industry should also make sacrifices, but on what principle can he take this position when he and his colleagues in the Government make no sacrifices, but, on the contrary, dissipate the resources of the country without regard to the question as to whether there is a war on or not? My hon. friend last year asked this Parliament to support a proposition to give $8,000,000 out of the treasury when we are spending our blood and treasure in war, in order to get the support of the hon. member for Charlevoix and Saguenay (Sir Rodolphe Forget). Will the hon. gentleman have the temerity and audacity to come to this Parliament and ask us to permit him to take $8,000,000 from the treasury and hand it over to that hon. gentleman? If my hon. friend expects that the people are going to be impressed by the appeals made to them for sacrifice and patriotism in face of an action of that kind and repeated after fair warning was given by one of the judges in the courts of this country, I think he will find that he has misjudged the temper of the people. I could take my hon. fniend through other avenues of expenditure. He has kept on expending. He has spent no less than $17,000,000 on the Hudson Bay enterprise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly.

Certainly. Why
should my hon. friend increase and not diminish that expenditure at this time?

I asked a question in this House not lone aeo. in fact, since we came back, and some one representing some department gave me the statement that $17,000,000 was expended to 1917, and that the expenditure in the last financial year was in the vicinity of $4,000,000.
I see that they are asking $3,000,000 more for the Hudson' Bay railway this year in the main estimates. There is not much reduction about that?
The hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) had better explain what it is that he proposes to do with this $3,000,000. Is he going to take that out of this new taxation this year?

speechtext: What is the use of asking for it if it is not going to be spent?
