speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What is the use of asking for that which it is not prpr posed to spend? How much of the sum that

you are asking Parliament for do you not propose to spend?
He says the total amount will not be spent; there may be $50 left.

Apparently we are going to have that same old story which was given to us last year; when items in the estimates came up for consideration we were accustomed to hear hon. gentlemen say that they were not going to spend the money. We accepted the assurances of the Government last year in regard to a very large number of items and it was found that a great deal of the money was spent. We have the statement of the Minister of Customs that the work on the Hudson Bay railway has been stopped, but my hon. friend is an old Parliamentarian and he has the verv ingenious way of 5 p.m. throwing out a little aside like that for the purpose of breaking the force of an argument. But, in the face of the estimates which .show that they are asking for $3,000,000 to spend this year on this road, there is no sense in this Government making appeals to the people to sacrifice themselves in the way of taxation and service. The Minister of Finance tries to justify his excess business profits tax by declaring that his programme is one that ought to appeal to a particular class in war time but while making this appeal my hon. friend displays the most absolute disregard of the economies, and he has failed to appreciate and take home to himself and his colleagues the lesson that he gives to the rest of the people. In view- of that, I say once more that the minister ought to present a well-considered plan of taxation in regard to the people of Canada and not hit at one particular class, especially when he could deal with accumulated wealth. My hon. friend comes along when we are passing through the greatest period of stress in the war, and tells us that posterity will have to pay the bill, but that in the meantime he is going to tax industry and capital to a certain extent and along certain lines. He has no formulated plan, no policy, no organization, no proposal which he can present to this Parliament in a sensible and practical way. Had the hon. gentleman and his colleagues, instead of merely generalising the efforts of the people of this country, assigned to their proper avocations those different forces which the country possesses, they would have done something to make effective the country's efforts in behalf of the great cause in wdiich we are

engaged. The Minister of Finance falls short of his part. He says: Posterity will pay, but we will tax for the moment industry and capital. The Government go on spending just the same as they were doing in the past, and then they come to this Parliament, and when an hon. gentleman asks that Parliament should be given information as to where they got the money out of this tax, from whom they got it, and where excess profits were disclosed by the information collected by the Government, we cannot g'et that information though we desire it for the consideration of this question. It seems to me that the occasion is one that demands from the Finance Minister a reorganization of the whole financial programme and a consideration of the question as to the responsibility for our share of what we ought to pay for the war in this period of prosperity. My hon. friend ought to deal with this question in a systematic and practical way so as to place the burden on the proper shoulders. That broad way would have a better result and a more earnest application of effort upon all lines to the great questions that lie before us.

I would like to point out to the minister what seems to be a hardship. Assuming that a munition man started business, say, last year, and had to invest half a million dollars in plant, and the war did not last more than a year, would the minister allow, in making out the statement, sufficient depreciation on that plant before the profits were declared to enable the proprietor to come out whole at the end of the year? How many years would he consider it fair to apply that depreciation on account of plant, because practically it will be of no value when the making of munitions ceases? If a company started last year with $200,000 or $300,000 capital, invested $500,000 in plant, and made a profit of 75 per cent on the capital invested, would the minister first allow a reasonable depreciation, so that in the event of the business being closed up at the end of the war, the capital would not be taken to make up the loss in depreciation? It seems to me that it is a fair proposition, and that the public and capital should know that from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
When I use the words " net profits " I mean net profits after taking off a proper amount in respect of depreciation. The question of depreciation is a matter of fact in each ease,
and industry, in making returns, should in connection with its statement, indicate the amount which, having regard to the nature of the business, should be written off, for depreciation. Then we have to consider whether or not that is a proper allowance. Each case must be determined on its own merits. In other words, the question of depreciation is one of fact.

A statement was made by the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea), I think on Tuesday last when the committee were considering the resolution. That hon. gentlemen discussed in a very interesting and forceful manner the action of the Government in fixing the price of paper to the public. It was an interesting statement to me, bcause certain features were disclosed which were before that unknown to me. That hon. gentleman made the statement that paper was being sold to the trade in Canada to-day at a loss. His statement has (been confirmed to-day or yesterday by Mr- J. R. Booth of Ottawa, according to a statement in the press. I say that if that statement is correct, an injustice is being done to one branch of industry in this country, and I should like to have a statement from the Minister of Finance with respect to this matter. At least it would be fair for me to say that if their prices are fixed and it is true that they are selling to the trade at a loss, there should be some compensation to that industry in respect to taxation of their excess profits in other branches of the trade. I think that when the Government undertakes to fix the price of any commodity, that price, so fixed, should be just; if not it will work an injury to that particular trade and cause dissatisfaction. The member for Sherbrooke intimated rather plainly, I think, that the Minister of Finance was a little alarmed at the political influence of the newspapers if he did not succumb to their suggestions to fix the price. We have very excellent authority for that statement from another hon. gentleman. It might be said that the member for (Sherbrooke is somewhat prejudiced in hie statement because he is himself a manufacturer of paper, and that therefore hie statement might not be entitled to very great weight in respect to this particular question. But the late Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes), more than an ordinary individual, has had something to say about this matter, and when I find so disinterested a gentleman expressing the same view, I think it is time for the Minister of Finance candidly

and frankly to explain his position. The late Minister of Militia publicly and in recent days has stated that the Minister of Finance and Sir George Perley, the Minister of Militia overseas, have attempted to create an atmosphere against him for the purpose of driving 'him out of political life; and one of the influences which was used by the Minister of Finance, according to the late Minister of Militia, was the newspapers. The hon. member (Sir Sam Hughes) says that one of the avenues by which the Minister of Finance hoped to secure, this influence with the press was by fixing the price of paper. Perhaps it would be as well that I should give to the House just what the late Minister of Militia did say, because this statement does not come from an ordinary member of Parliament, but from one who has a national reputation in a great many respects. In speaking to his constituents, not very long ago, he said- and I should like to hear from the Minister of Finance as to this:
Another plan or scheme seems to have been the sweetening of the newspapers of Canada by departing from the first principles of the National policy to secure printing paper at fixed price, and incidentally benefit to a considerable extent the Yankee newspapers. The rich advertisements by brokers, by the Government, paid for by the poor people of Canada in connection with loans, also tended to mollify criticism of the press, and secure neutral, if not favourable consideration and comment.
I should hardly like to believe that the Minister of Finance was a party to the dictation of paper prices from the motives designated by the hon. member for Victoria. If that is correct, I say it is unjust. If the Minister of Finance thinks the member for Victoria is incorrect, that this statement is unfair, I should like to have him say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have too much respect for the press of Canada, both Liberal and Conservative, to seriously argue in this House a question as to whether they would use their great influence to obtain some business advantage for themselves. The representatives of the press of this country, without any distinction of political affiliation, came to me, as they had a perfect right to do, and asked me to consider a matter which was of the utmost importance to them in their business. They pointed out that the prevailing rates for newsprint paper were such that if -they were obliged to pay them their industry would be ruined. That was a proper subject for them to bring to my attention, and it was a proper subject 
for me, as minister, to consider. It was considered, as I said,' in the House the other day, and, after exhausting all the arts of persuasion in endeavouring to get the question between the manufacturers of newsprint paper and the press settled, we took the action that is known to the House. I may say that this action was taken after we had, through our Tariff Board, made as careful an investigation as we could as to the increased cost of manufacture to the newsprint producers. The situation in regard to cost in all manufactures is a changing one from week to week during the progress of the war. A short time ago, in order that we might have full information as to the situation, we appointed Mr. R. A. Pringle, K.C., for the purpose of investigating the cost of production and all the conditions surrounding the manufacture and sale of newsprint paper in Canada. I submit to the House that, in view of the conditions brought to our attention by the press, the action which we have taken was a proper course for any Government to take in the premises. I may say that the investigation which is now proceeding will, I believe, meet the wishes of the manufacturers themselves as well as of the newspapers, because they desired to draw to our attention facts which they regard as of importance in connection with the price which they may be permitted to charge for newsprint paper. A,s to my hon. friend's general statement with regard to myself and the press, I would point out that the ex-Minis

ter of Militia had resigned before the decision as to fixing the cost of newsprint paper had been reached by the Government. There would be no connection, therefore, such as my hon. friend suggests as between cause and effect.

In discussing the business profits tax, the hon. member for South Renfrew pointed out that the manufacturers who under the present extraordinary conditions were earning large profits could not tell when those profits would be cut off. Many of the factories now engaged in the manufacture of munitions and other war supplies were doing other business previous to the outbreak of war; they simply readapted their machinery and converted their plants in such manner as to make them capable of producing munitions. The amount of depreciation in respect of such industries would not be so great as in the case of those which went into business in the. first instance for the sole purpose of manufacturing munitions and war supplies.
I understood the minister to say that in

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
submitting their statements to the department, firms were allowed to estimate the amount of depreciation, and it was for the department to determine whether the depreciation estimated was fair and proper.
I was going to ask, before the minister answ'exed the question regarding depreciation, whether a fixed ratio of depreciation was allowed by the department in all cases.
I can conceive that such an arrangement would be hardly fair to such industries and factories as my hon. friend (Mr. Loggie) has referred to.
I suggest, then, that the depreciation in respect of factories which have been equipped for the special purpose of manufacturing munitions or supplies which are peculiarly incidental to the conduct of the war would be larger than that of the factory which simply has to readjust itself to.former conditions after the war is over. My hon. friend referred to the remarks of the hon. member for Pictou concerning the criticisms directed by the press against the tax rate suggested under these proposals. I agree that certain papers, which are behind the interests mostly affected, severely criticise the proposed taxation, but the press at large admit that the principle of the taxation is along the right lines. Whether or not it is excessive is a question for the House to determine. It is Dossible that in view of the increasing demand for the product of these factories, very large extensions to the plants may be necessary. These extensions will involve an investment of capital which will be productive of return only for a short period; consequently a very large amount may have to be written off for depreciation. Moreover, a firm might find itself embarrassed if, in order to pay these taxes, it had to use monev that would otherwise be used for extension of plant. No matter what decision may ultimately be arrived at, it must be evident to all that it would be a very serious thing if, by reason of the imposition of a tax or of any action taken by the Government, any industry should be retarded or embarrassed. I am quite satisfied that the Government has no intention of taking such action, but I submit that this is a matter which should seriously engage its attention before the question is finally disposed of. .

When the Minister of Finance put into force the additional 71 per cent duty, he promised us that the statistical departments would disclose in the annual statements just what amount came from free goods and what from application of the 71 per cent to the general tariff. That statement has never very clearly appeared, and I think that it is in the general interest that the information should appear in the Customs and Trade and Commerce returns. I obtained some figures from the Customs returns and used them during the debate upon the Budget. Although they were not later contradicted, at the time I made the statement some hon. gentlemen opposite seemed disposed to question them. For instance I find that the total Customs war tax for the fiscal year 1915-16, as given on page 192 of the Customs return, was $21,814,000. I assume that that was the amount of revenue recovered from the 71 per cent tax on dutiable and free goods. During that year there was an importation of $254,000,000 worth of goods formerly free. If those goods paid an import tax of 71 per cent, the amount paid into the treasury would be $19,000,000. This would further show that the amount of revenue recoverable by the 71 per cent tariff on dutiable goods amounted to only $2,000,000. The minister this afternoon stated that the tptal amount of revenue received from the 71 per cent tariff tax for the year just closed amounted to $37,000,000, $20,000,000 of which was attributable to the tariff on free goods and the balance to the surtax on dutiable goods.
If the figures to which I have referred for the fiscal year 1915-16 are correct, I doubt very much the accuracy of the figures which the minister has given this afternoon. I have always doubted the wisdom of applying the 71 per cent increase to the dutiable list; in fact, I have always protested against it. I have never believed it to be in the commercial interest of the country, and I doubt very much if it gives us any "substantial revenue. The point, however, that I wish to make at the present time is to urge that those figures be carefully kept, and that they appear in a prominent place in our statistical returns, so that we may have an opportunity of knowing just what is the effect of the imposition of the 71 per cent tax on dutiable and non-dutiable goods.

I have not looked into the matter especially, but it was my intention that the information should appear in the customs returns, and I think I so stated to the House at the time that I introduced the Budget in 1915 or in the discussions in connection with that Budget. Although my hon. friend usually presents his statements as c'early as any other hon.

member, I have never been able to follow him in what I take to be his assertion that we have derived no revenue in respect of the 7i per cent increase in the general tariff. Of course you get some revenue, but the general effect of the 7J per cent increase is to prohibit importations, and the net result is that you would have secured more revenue if you had not applied the increase at all. That is what I mean.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry that I am not able to give my hon. friend the information, and that is the reason I did not see the relevancy, if he will pardon me for saying so, of the argument which he put forward. My hon. friend must have the information for some years. What year is it for which my hon. friend has the information?

speechtext: Practically the whole of 1915-two years ago.
Is that the financial year which ended in 1916?

Has my hon. friend no data gathered that would enable him to predict how much the application of this extra rate yielded in the financial year 1915-16?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry to say to my hon. friend that the data would not be useful to us in reaching the amount, and for this reason: in the first place, there were some concerns that made little or no money during 1914-15, because that was the period of dislocation succeeding the outbreak of the war, but some of those companies, I think, have done very well this last year. I reach that conclusion by reason of the conditions that have prevailed in the country, and I assume that those companies will make large profits. Other concerns that made large profits on the outbreak of war will not make so much during the last accounting period, for the reason that they had large supplies of goods or commodities on hand which appreciated in value when the war broke out. Some grain companies for instance, made large profits in the year succeeding the outbreak of the war, because their commodities appreciated in value very considerably on account of the war. As to how they will have done this year I am unable to say, because I have not the returns.

It would be a matter of great importance to the House and to the country if the minister would give an accurate statement of the figures as to which my hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Loggie) has made an estimate. I think this committee, dealing with taxation and considering what is the best method by which the finances of the country in connection with the tremendous burdens imposed on account of the war shall be raised, and all the other matters which are germane to that, should know how much money the Minister of Finance has raised out of the extra taxes during the last two years. My hon. friend ought to be able to get that information without much difficulty, and I should like him to give us the assurance that he will place it before the House after dinner, or at some other time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would have to be simply an estimate. In the first place we know that the tariff produced $37,000,000. In the second place we know that the first year of the excess business profits tax produced $12,500,000; I do not know what the figures for the second and last periods will be. My hon. friend also estimates about $66,000,000 from post office and excise returns. 'My own idea would be that from $60,000,000 to $65,000,000 would be a fair estimate, and which my hon. friend will not fail to observe is about the amount we set aside for reducing the principal of our war debt. In addition to that, we paid the increased interest, and the pensions.

Resolution agreed to.
On resolution No. 2:

speechtext:
This section is
to Temove any doubt as to the amount accumulated profits which would b.e 'allowed as capital. We allow the amount which has accumulated at the commencement of the accounting period. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is merely
an amendment to the Act. I think my hon. friend was out when I explained why it was necessary to enact this second section. We defined capital last year <as including unimpaired reserve and accumulated profits. We had in mind at the time that that would mean accumulated profits at the commencement of an accounting period, but one or two firms have set up that they should he allowed to take profits every month or so during the term, and compute the

seven per cent on those. A company, let us say, at the commencement of an accounting period has a certain unimpaired reserve, a certain capital and a certain amount of accumulated profits. We claim that in calculating the profits the seven per cent should be upon those three things, capital, unimpaired reserve, and accumulated profits at the commencement of the term, and this amendment is simply to effectuate the intention we had at that time. The Act will be administered accordingly.

I am sure that any one who read the debates last year must have got the impression that my hon, friend was proposing taxation which would, last to the end of the three year period. I think if my hoA. friend will read Hansard of last year he will find that he almost expressly said that the taxation he then proposed was final for the three year period. I am very much opposed to retroactive legislation except for the purpose of correcting a manifest mistake, and while it is within the power of Parliament at all times to-pass legislation remedying conditions that may have resulted from previous enactments, I am sure my hon. friend will agree with me that the wisest policy for a prudent minister to follow is to avoid retroactive legislation if at all possible. I think the minister will be bound to admit that, whether intentionally or not-and I think it was with the very best intentions-he gave the impression to the country and to the parties directly affected that the scheme of taxation he proposed last year was a finality for the three year period, so far as this method of taxation is concerned. I will not repeat the arguments I ventured to make earlier in the day, but I think the minister should have presented to Parliament a comprehensive system of taxation dealing with all the necessities of the war at the present time. Retroactive legislation such as my hon. friend proposes is not wise or justifiable legislation, and I think the minister should explain to the House why he proposes retroactive legislation of this character.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
The minister has
dealt with only one phase of the subject. He has not told us whether I am correct in my statement that he had declared that this class of people would not be called upon for more taxes during the three-year period. Certainly, the impression one gets from reading Hansard of last year, as well as one's recollection of the debate, is that the minister was not coming back to this particular form of taxation during this period. I need not quote what I have under my hand; the minister repeatedly stated that later on the necessities of the country under war conditions might necessitate other forms of taxation, hut he just as clearly indicated that he was pot coming back to this particular class of taxation, that he would not increase the taxes upon these people within the term fixed by this law. I think he will admit that that is the effect of his statement, and I think he should tell us why he comes back to these same people for more money instead of seeking other avenues of taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member (Mr. Macdonald) raises a wider question. My statement as I made it, and as it is reported in Hansard, is clear. I stated that this tax would be limited to a period of three years; I did not say that it would not he increased. The action now taken is not inconsistent with my statement of last year. But even suppose-though I do not admit it as a matter of fact-that my statement was as the hon. member understood it, the fact remains that this is a time of war. Governments in war time must, from time to time, take such action as they deem in the public interest. Personally, I should be the first to favour giving force and effect to any undertaking that a minister might

give. I did state that this tax was limited to a period of three years, and I repeat that. The hon. gentleman may ask me: is it your intention to renew it next year? My answer is: No. And for this reason-I did undertake that the tax should he for a three-year term, but I did not undertake that it should not be changed and modified. In the nature of things, at the end of this year, even if the war is not ended, we must be comparatively close to the end of it. I stated when the subject was under discussion before that a tax of this kind, while an eminently proper one for war time, is not a good taxation measure for a peace time. It is not well that there should be fear of a business tax in time of peace, because that is the time when we desire capital to flow into the country and when a severe tax on profits may injure business. That is one reason why I do not share the apprehensions of those who say that this tax is going to do the country considerable damage. No Minister of Finance desires to impose taxation, even excess profits taxation. But an excess profits tax is a very fair tax, and, if limited to a certain period so that business men may know that it is comins to an end, it does no great injustice.
The hon, member for Pietou has contrasted our taxation proposals as to the money invested in business and as to the money invested for income purposes by individuals. But he has overlooked one very important point. So far as I know, there are verv few men in Canada with a capital of, say, $100,000 who derive any more than six per cent by way of income upon that capital. Now, on capital invested in business we exempt the profits up to seven per cent, and from seven to fifteen per cent all we take is one-quarter. So that, logically, there is no discrimination against capital invested in business, because the tax applies only upon excess profits in business. If we were bringing down a taxation measure which took a portion of the capital invested in business, I would be the first to agree with my hon. friend that there >
was a discrimination against business in favour of those who have put their capital into some other investment.
But money invested in business emplovs labour and helps on the industries of the coumtrv. while accumulated wealth from which an interest income is derived lies inert.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not agree with my hon. friend there. The revenue
derived from investment bv men who have large incomes does find its way back into productive industry. Very often, these men are holders of bonds and shares in industrial companies. Another thing which I pointed out the other nieht is this: an income tax would fall very heavily upon the men who are immediately affected by it. Suppose that my hon. friend is a majority shareholder in a company subject to this tax. I need not tell him as a lawyer that the amount paid to the Government under the provisions of this Bill could be distributed to the shareholders by the directors. Does it help a company that is subject to this tax if, in addition to taxing their shareholders, I impose an income tax upon those shareholders? This is ground that we have gone over two or three times, and I am sorry to bring it again to the attention of the House, but the statements of my hon. friend from Pietou seem to call for a reply.
The fact remains that in all our cities there are men who escape taxation absolutely at present. That is the complaint of the country. What does the minister say to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The capital in industrial companies and in business' of all kinds escapes taxation up to seven per cent, and over seven per cent we take only a percentage. This excess profits tax has been criticised, but we must remember that nearly all nations are resorting to this tax, as a proper one. In England, the excess profits tax is very severe. The principle is that, being excess profits made during the war, the state must take a substantial share of it. As I say, I believe that this is a good measure in time of war, but not in time of peace. I never would think of imposing it in time of peace; let the ordinary law of Supply and demand govern then. In time of peace all the things that influence that law have full force and play; but that is not true in war time, for then industries make abnormal profits; they make, it may be, fifty or even a hundred per cent where formerly they made no more than five or six per cent. It seems to me sound to take the profits of companies which profits are undoubtedly due to war conditions. I think that is a principle recognized by all the belligerent countries.

I do not say that
the minister should not have a business profits tax; the point I make is that he

should go further and open up other avenues of taxation. In Britain the business profit taxes are only a modicum of total taxation. Taxation there reaches accumulated wealth. They have reached landed proprietors and the hereditary wealth of the country. The United States scheme of taxation, while it has business profits included in it, does not rest upon that source alone. They deal with income, with accumulated wealth and with a great many new sources of taxation, an example of which my hon. friend would have been wise to have followed this year instead of practically going back upon the position which he took last year, namely, that the proposed taxation would last for three years. He should have gone to other sources this year because the taxation which is paid by the business people of this country is so extraordinary and unusual that it is bound to create an onerous condition of such a character as will impair and interfere with industries. That is the criticism I make in regard to the policy but not in regard to the principle of the Business Profits Tax itself.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I find, on looking into the situation in the United States, that, although they are proposing to raise very much more revenue from the business profits tax, they have not attempted anything like the excessive measure proposed by my hon. friend. In the United States the taxation Bill recognizes the right of the business man, corporation or firm to have S per cent of revenue on the amount invested, and the former business tax involved an imposition of only 8 per cent of the amount over that. Under war conditions this year the -additional taxation imposed is only another 8 per cent, or 16 per cent of the amount, no matter what it may be. That is very much less than my hon. friend proposes. Not only that, but in England the taxation is placed upon the real excess profits. My hon. friend assumes that, in war times and in peace times alike, the manufacturer has no business to earn more than 10 per cent on his investment without giving some of it to the public. In England a comparison is made between the present profit of a company and the profit made by it in peace times, and

the imposition is made upon the excess which comes as a result of the war, what might properly be called war profits. My hon. friend takes no consideration of the fact that there should be a difference between peace times and war times. He taxes without regard to the difference in profits during peace and war. For that reason, I submit that my hon. friend has gone too far in his proposal. A* very wise writer on this question of taxation, particularly war taxation, lays down the principle that tax

ation should be economically wise and should be such taxation as is compatible with the continuance of, active enterprise and is calculated not to slacken the industry or dampen the loyalty or patriotism of the citizen. To that proposition no exception can be taken. But my hon. friend's proposals do not come under that proposition, and the exactions he is taking will slacken the industry, impair the prospect of capital investment, and dampen the patriotic enthusiasm of the party who is being taxed.
In regard to income tax, upon which the minister has shifted his ground several times, it would be interesting to see how the income tax proposals of the United States work out. Under the original law for the taxation of incomes which has been on the statute book for quite a period of years, no income under $5,000 is taxed. An exemption was made of $2,000 for the heads of families. Under the law of last year, September 10, for the first time and in the face of the entrance of the nation into the war, we find provision for the taxation of incomes of $3,000, and from these $20 a year is taken. From the $4,000 man, $40 is taken, and from the $5,000 man, $60 is taken. The $10,000 man practically contributes $200, and then for each amount of $15,000,	$20,000, $25,000, $45,000 and
$50,000 a year the amount of taxation increases gradually until the $50,000 man pays approximately $4,000 a year to the state. As the income increases to $150,000, the tax increases to $24,220 under the new law, and parties in receipt of incomes greater than that amount pay on a very much higher scale, until the man with an income of $1,000,000 pays $380,000 a year to the state. My hon. friend could very well begin taxing people who are in receipt of $20,000 a year and over. My hon. friend has failed to approach the problem of taxation for the war on a scientific basis; he is outlining no definite plan by which all parties in .the state should contribute in accordance with their ability to do so. He

is simply dealing with temporary expedients, the effect of which we have already pointed out. But if my hon. friend is at all prepared to consider this question, there is no reason why an income tax should not be framed for dealing with amounts lower than that if it is to be made a matter of permanent policy, and I reserve all statements in regard to what might be done under a permanent policy. I want to point out to my hon. friend that there are hundreds of men in this country, if not thousands, who are in receipt of incomes of $20,000 a year and more, and there is no reason why my hon. friend should not, through the machinery he has at hand, reach those people and compel them to pay. He could take $1,000 a year from a man earning $20,000 a year or upwards. But my hon. friend has set his face against that for numerous reasons which he has given from time to time, and the only virtue one can have in referring to the matter is to point out what my 'hon. friend might do which he has left undone. There is another question:	My hon. friend seems
to think that he should not lay before Parliament a statement of the amounts he has received from the men who have furnished data in regard to the business tax, that all data in regard to it should be withheld from the consideration of this House and the country. I am at a loss to know why that should be so. Of course, my hon. friend intimates that if we move in the House for that information he will consider what he will do, but I have to point out that in the United States that data is made public. There is no such reservation there. For instance, I find in the papers of the United States information which could only be obtained from the public records dealing with business profits there, that for the year 1915, 366,433 corporations made income returns, of which, however, 172,532 reported operating deficits. The yield of this tax assessed on corporations, on the basis of returns filed, was $51,844,422. It is estimated that the return from the additional taxation would .amount to~ at least $200,000,000 more. If, in the gTeat nation to the south of us, with all its ramifications of corporation work, it is not found that an injury to the public interest is caused by giving to the world a statement of returns furnished by these corporations in answer to a taxing law, on what possible basis can it be urged that we should not have the same information furnished in Canada? The consideration suggested by my hon. friend 105
from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) this afternoon seemed to 'be overpowering. In the United States, the great bulk of extra money required for the war is not expected to be made from the business profits source, as my hon. friend is making it solely in Canada, but from the income 'source, from the .accumulated wealth; whereas they expect to get only $250,000,000 from the business profits source in the United States, the estimates of the income tax run from $500,000,000 to $700,000,000.
Before these resolutions pass, therefore, my hon. friend should consider the advisability of changing his proposal in some way. It is the very reverse of scientific. It is class legislation; it will interfere with industry and with, the investment of capital and leave absolutely untouched the accumulated wealth pf Canada-the source from which the nation should draw in such a time as this. Hundreds of millionaires in Canada ought to be made pay. My hon. friend will have no difficulty in reaching them; the efficient tax collector who had to do with the business profits tax will look after it if my hon. friend will give him the full authority.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In referring to the proposed United States business profits tax, my hon. friend overlooks the fact that the United States has not been at war for three years. The United States has had three years of prosperity such as she never before experienced in her history. Congress is considering a taxation measure for present needs, but my hon. friend would hesitate to predict what degree of taxation the United States may resort to before the war is over, especially if it lasts another three years. Canada baa organized an expeditionary force of over 400,000 men. If my hon. friend will multiply that number by 13 they having 13 times our population he will find that a corresponding effort on the part of the United States would result in the organization of a military force of 5,000,000 men. So that in criticising the taxation measure which the (Government lays betftone 'the House, the position of the United States in respect to taxation, having Tegard to the stage at which they have arrived in the war, is no criterion by which we should be guided. When this war broke out I did not immediately propose an excess profits tax. In August 1914, we brought down a mild measure of taxation; we raised the excise duties upon liquors, cigars and tobaccos, as well as the duties upon sugar and certain other commodities. Tn 1915



we raised, the tariff to 7J per cent and 5 per cent-the United States proposes to raise the tariff 10 per cent at this stage. Then we introduced the other measures of taxation with which hon. gentlemen are familiar; so that we have been progressive in our taxation measures. The action of Congress at this time, therefore, is not a criterion by which our measure should be judged or upon which we should act. My hon. friend has suggested that we should tax incomes of $20,000 and over. I am positive that if I brought in any such measure my hon. friend would be foremost in criticising it as most unjust to a limited <dass of individuals. He would have the tax limited to incomes of $2,000 or $3,000. My hon. friend would oppose any measure of taxation that we should bring in; it would make no difference what it was. He has one advantage over most of us, whether on this iside or on the other side: he was born a partisan. Any measure of taxation, therefore, proposed by the Government would meet with the opposition of my hon. friend. He complains that we are letting the millionaires off, but his criticism this afternoon has been largely -I will not say at the instance of, but he has had them in mind-in respect of large firms or establishments that can well afford to pay this tax. The Nova Scotia Steel & Coal Company is in my -hon. friend's constituency; I should not be surprised if he had that firm particularly in mind. I know Mr. Cantley well enough to be sure that he does not mind paying taxes for war purposes upon the profits of the company which, I am glad to say, have been considerable since the outbreak of -the war. My hon. friend has been trying to ride two horses this afternoon, and he has not been successful. He has been saying, during the course of this discussion, that he is in favour, of the excess profits tax, but he has been criticising it because he knows that there is some dissatisfaction because it is fairly -severe. Why does my hon. friend not say either that he is in favour of a severe excess profits tax, or that he is not? He will not do that, because he is attempting to ride two -horses at the same time.
What kind of horse is my -hon. friend riding?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only horse I am trying to ride is the horse that will win this war-a war-horse. That is a pretty good steed to ride.
My hon. friend is not riding it very well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member for Pictou is trying to ride an election horse; that is the difference. My hon-. friend referred to the British tax. The British taxation measure on excess profits realized about $800,000,000-and they have six times as many people as we have. The hon. gentleman says that our tax is excessive, yet the hon. member for Dauphin said the other night: why do you not take $200,000,000 out of the manufacturers? Why does my hon. friend from Pictou not criticise the member for DauDhin? On the one hand hon. gentlemen opposite say: you are taxing the manufacturers too much; and on the other: you are not taxing them enough. I will not say that that is the attitude of all hon. gentlemen opposite, because that would be unjust, but it is the attitude of some. In England the excess profits tax is levied, as the member for Pictou has indicated, on the difference between the profits in war time and the profits over a three year period preceding the war. As a result, a number of businesses in England that were making small profits before the war broke out, due to the unsettled conditions-because tight money had prevailed for a considerable period before the war-are bearing an undue proportion of the excess profits tax. Companies that were earning from 25 to 50 per cent before the war are paying nothing or very little, whereas companies which were earning only 5 or 6 per cent and are now earning from 25 to 40 per cent, are paying into the British treasury 80 per cent of the difference.

Would it not be reasonable to attribute to the war the excess profits of those companies which were not earning much before the war broke out and, vice versa, to attribute to the adverse effect of the war the decrease in the profits of -many companies which were doing well before the war broke out?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is what I think they had in mind, but in the operation of the legislation the greatest injustice results to many businesses. I have been told by business men of the highest standing that the British tax is ineauitable, unjust, and unfair for the reasons given-. Only the other day at Washington , a representative British manufacturer who was carrying on business in a large way said: We had a run of hard luck the year before the war; we are now taxed on a tremendous scale. He complained bitterly of the in-

justice of the British system and said that our taxation was much fairer. I am only giving hon. gentlemen the view of some of the business men of England with respect to the business profits tax over there. My hon. friend snoke of the furnishing of information with regard to the returns. The information in respect of this accounting period will not be available until 1918. With regard to the years 1915, 1916 and 1917, personally, I should favour bringing down a blue book, giving the names of the firms and the amount of their taxation, at the ensuing session of Parliament, but the taxation returns for 1914-15 are fairly complete. If any hon. member desires information with respect to a particular industry or a firm engaged in a particular industry, the proper course is for that member to place upon the Order Paper a request for the information which he desires, and then we can decide whether or not that information should be furnished. So far as I am concerned, I believe in the fullest possible disclosure in regard to any matter in my office unless the public interest stands in the way. In the administration pi any custom tax or any other tax, if this House desires information and it appears that the request on the Order Paper is not contrary to the public interest, so far as I am concerned, I would be prepared to bring down the information.

Did my hon. friend take into consideration in the excess profits tax that when the war is over and things go back to normal, some of those firms which are at the present time making a large profit might be affected very adversely by the 75 per cent tax in accumulating a reserve that would assist in carrying them over, I shall not say the hard times, but the less remunerative times? It would be advantageous for a good many of those firms to pile up a reasonable reserve to carry them over the dull times that we may be approaching, When the war is over and when many of those firms which are making munitions have to turn their attention once more to their former lines of business, there will be very serious times for themselves and for their employees unless they have sufficient reserves to carry them over the transition pexipd.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry my
hon. friend was not in the House this afternoon, because I dealt with that matter very fully in reply to remarks of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham),
but I will briefly rehearse the statement which I made. In the first place the Business Profits War Tax comes to an end at the end of this year, and the present taxation proposals apply only to the last accounting period of the three year period covered by the legislation. Secondly, with regard to many of the businesses in Canada, the last accounting period has already expired, and from this period, pi course, their profits are not subject to the taxation. Thirdly, the tax has been levied for a period of three years. For the first year all we took was one-quarter of the net profits over seven per cent; for the second year, we also took only one-quarter over seven per cent, and the second year was a good year for all businesses in Canada. The third year has also been a good year for nearly all businesses in Canada, and it is from that third year's profits that we are taking this increased amount of taxation. It is not as if we were taking all their excess profits; we are leaving them very substantial sums. My opinion has been that the position of most companies in Canada is pretty liquid. There are many companies, however, which have made betterments and improvements, and a good deal of the profits have gone back into those betterments and improvements and into stock. If it would be proper to consider, in connection with depreciation, a reasonable allowance where plants have been unduly extended during the war period, that might be a fair subject of consideration. I have no particular cases in view. I simply say that if a plant has been built to a great extent over what might be regarded as the normal requirements in order to handle the business of the war, that might be a subject of fair consideration with regard to the amount written off for depreciation.
Then we come to the other aspect of the case as to whether the companies will be able to raise the money to pay the tax. This tax is not due until 1918, and as I say, the Business Tax comes to an end this year, and we are not pressing any firms unduly as to payment. We expect them to pay when the payments are due in accordance with the measure which was passed by the House last year, but the penalty is not a high rate of interest, and I am quite sure there will be no ground for the accusation that the taxation has been harshly enforced upon firms that could not raise the money to pay it. That is only a question of reasonable administration. I think, therefore, on all these grounds there is no

reason for apprehension that firms are going to be forced into bankruptcy. I am sure that I would be the last man to consider favourably a measure that would have that effect.

I have not the slightest doubt that the minister fully intends that this tax will end in the accounting periods of those firms in this year, and that this later proposed tax will apply only for this year; but my hon. friend, like the rest of us, does not control the war, and there is no doubt that after this year there will have to be revenue derived from some source to pay the expenses of the war. While my hon. friend applies the tax only for this year and while perhaps for the moment he does not intend to apply it for a further period, still he can not cease imposing some excess taxation even if the war should come to an end this year. I do not therefore, see, although he may fully intend that the excess profits tax will cease this year and the payment cease next year, how he can promise that definitely. I do not grasp that .at all, because he is in the hands of powers over which he has no control. Therefore, while he may give the companies an opportunity to pay, at the same time I fear that a great hardship wilt be imposed on some people. Had my hon. friend seen the wisdom of reducing the amount of taxation or of making every one pay their fair share, I would have suggested to him that, if he thought seven per cent was too low an amount for firms with a capital of less than $50,000, he might increase that to a certain extent, that is, he might allow them to earn eight per cent for instance, without imposing taxation. The other night he said in reply to me that the amount that a firm with a capital of $40,000 would earn at seven per cent would not be very great, but in answer to that I would suggest that perhaps he could increase the amount that would be allowed and still at the same time collect a certain amount of taxation from every one in this country who is engaged in business and making a profit. One man has as much right to pay taxes as another. I would suggest to my hon. friend that instead of having the fifty per cent tax apply on earnings of from fifteen to twenty per cent, he should make it apply on earnings of from fifteen to thirty per cent, and make the	higher	rate of taxation	applyon	profits	over	thirty per	cent.At the same time I would advocate that 	.
there be a spread downwards, so as to take in everybody and make the taxation as equitable as possible. I know my hon. friend says that it would cost too much to collect taxes from firms with a lower capitalization than $50,000, but I do not think it would cost a great deal to send notices from the department to people in every line of business asking them to send in a statement of their business affairs. I believe the bulk of the people are perfectly willing to pay their share of taxation, and I think most of them would send in these particulars. I do not see why there should be any excessive cost in taxing firms with a lower capitalization than $50,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As I stated this afternoon, next year we shall in all probability be on the eve of peace. There is this further fact: we shall get the revenue which this measure will produce in the year 1918. I also stated this afternoon that I did not regard this excess profits tax as a good tax in time of peace, though it is a just tax in time of war. It has been adopted, so far as I know, by practically every one of the belligerent nations. It is not the intention to re-enact this measure. Another reason that I think is entitled to some weight is this: when we introduced the measure we set a limit of three years, and that understanding was acted upon by firms and companies establishing themselves here, and I therefore feel we are under an obligation in that respect.

I am sorry that the good-natured criticism I ventured to make this afternoon should have provoked so much resentment from the minister. Whenever the Minister of Finance gets into trouble, he does one of two things-he either mounts his aeroplane and soars into the realm of exchange, which he talks about in a mysterious manner as if it were a science that no other member of the House could venture to think about-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not feel quite certain that I understand it myself.

When my hon.
friend shrouds himself in the mystery of that science he thinks he has completely escaped from his pursuers. His other course is .to declare that he is winning the war. Let any one criticise the Minister of Finance and if he does not talk about exchange he will at once say that he is winning the war. He was winning the war when he gave Sir Rodolphe Forget $8,000,000 for the Quebec and Saguenay railway. The Min-

ister of Finance pretends to be an economist, but in the last four years he has spent $40,000,000 on public works and he raised the taxes to pay for these works on the pretense that the money was to be devoted to the war. These are facts about which there is no question. Then he spent $17,000,000 on the Hudson Bay railway. When hon. gentlemen on this side of the House discuss the measures of my hon. friend in a reasonable way, without acrimony of any kind, it is somewhat unusual, I think, for the Minister of Finance to attribute personal motives to us. My hon. friend should not be sc thin-skinned. I think he is entirely exceeding the courtesies of debate when he calls people partisan, and suggests that they are discussing his measures for the benefit of some particular industry. The views which I put forward this afternoon were based on arguments which I had a perfect right to present to the House, and there was nothing at all personal in my remarks.
The sum and substance of the whole discussion is this: My hon. friend intends to stand by this excess profits tax. My hon. friend says that the excess profits tax is a good tax in wartime, but not in peace time. Now, if the war stops next year the' tax will come off. We all wish that my hon. friend's prophecy in regard to the conclusion of the war may come true, after these long sad years of waiting, but the present outlook, which ie not altogether rosy, does not give one much hope that my hon. friend has any -sound basis for his conclusion. Does my hon. friend say that if the war is not over next year the tax will be discontinued?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, I stated that. I also said that if the war went on and our expenditures increased we should have to resort to new modes of taxation. My hon. friend has indulged in a little chiding, and he is the last man in the House who should indulge in that. When he gets up and talks about the expenditures of this country you would think he was a political Sir Galahad. You can almost see the wings sprouting from his shoulders when he gets up and talks about the expenditures this Government has made. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that since the war broke out this Government has gone on with only such public works as were absolutely necessary, and the greater part of our expenditure on public works has been on undertakings initiated in large measure by hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in
power. 1 have no desire to discuss these matters from a political standpoint; I allowed a -question of my hon. friend this afternoon to go unanswered simply because I did not want to get mixed up in a political discussion. When the war broke out there was an enormous amount of unemployment in this country, due to the dislocation of business. Money supplies for carrying on undertakings throughout the country were shut off at their source, and there was consequently a great deal of unemployment. Would it have been good policy for the Government to shut down on all public works at that time? That would have been most unwise. The policy we adopted was to go ahead with isuch public works as were under way; that was good sense; it was the right thing to do, and we did it. Just as soon as business conditions improved and unemployment decreased we adopted the opposite policy.
You stated this afternoon in answer to a question that you spent $15,000,000 on public works last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are works going on in this country which should not be stopped. My hon. friend has referred to the Hudson Bay railway. The hon. member for -South Renfrew, when he was Minister of Railways, let the contract for the building of that road, and I cannot recollect any session since 1911 when hon. gentle- * men opposite have not urged the Government to continue with the building of that road. The road has been gone on with, so far as I know, with the consent of both parties in -this House.
What does the hon. gentleman suggest? Here are terminals on Hudson. Bay half finished and"liable to go to pieces; here are rails lying rusting and a road unfinished and not used. Is the Government to stop work upon it altogether? Is that good common sense? We had to continue the construction of that road or suffer loss. It is wise, when you have an uncompleted undertaking, to go ahead with it at all events to the extent necessary to save wastage and loss. It would have been a most foolish policy to abandon altogether the Hudson Bay road.
But the Minister of Railways tells us that he contemplates stopping the construction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not stopped. True, there are only a comparatively few men on the work, as I have learned from the contractor. We have been carrying on

this enterprise only to the extent necessary to prevent national loss. The ereat part of our public works expenditures to which the hon. member refers are expenditures on ports and harbours. In this House last year request after request was made by hon. members opposite for the construction of this grain elevator, that dock, or the other pier-all necessary public works in their opinion. What we have done is to go ahead "with necessary public works.
What about the Quebec and Saguenay?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Who subsidized the Quebec and Saguenay originally? It was hon. gentlemen opposite. This Government found itself face to face with an uncompleted enterprise, and had to take action. The right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) did not oppose the measure that was passed last year. He knew that the city of Quebec and the district of Quebec were interested in the completion of that road. When we talk about burdens, I will say this-that the heaviest burdens we had were in connection with railways. We had to finish the National Transcontinental and we had to subsidize other roads to carry them on, but these roads were the result of the' policy of the previous Liberal Government. Since the outbreak of this war we have continually reduced the expenditure of the Dominion both on current account and on capital account. So far has that gone that the entire expenditure of the Dominion to-day, outside of the war, is less than it was three years ago, notwithstanding that there are embraced in that expenditure charges of $25,000,000 for interest on increased national debt, and pensions. We have endeavoured in every way to cut down expenditure, but it is not wise to cut down expenditure to such an extent as to impair the efficiency of the public service or cause waste in connection with enterprises already undertaken. Close down the work on the Welland Canal, some have told us. But that is a great public work which has been supported by both sides. I do not desire to enter into political controversy; there is no use in talking of the past, and political recrimination is wholly out of place at a time like this. But I felt I must say something in reply to the strictures passed upon the administration by the hon. member (Mr. Macdonald) this afternoon.

The hon. minister talks about cutting down the expenditure by 
$25,000,000 as compared with what it was two years ago; but he did not tell the committee that even when they are cut down by that $25,000,000, our public expenditures are fifty per cent higher now than they were when hon. gentlemen opposite took office five years age. Speaking of the Quebec and Saguenay Railway, he evidently wishes the committee to believe that the Liberal party was responsible for that enterprise. But the Liberal party had nothing to do with the sixty-five miles of the Forget railway for which the Minister of Finance is going to hand out about $8,000,000-for before he is through with it the expenditure will amount to about that. This is to complete a road that never can hope to earn operating expenses. And the expenditure is made in the middle of a war. He tries .to make it appear that this side of the House were responsible. We voted against that last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Some of you.

I know that I did; I voted against it because it was an absolutely um called for expenditure, wholly unjustified in any way, except politically-to put millions of dollars into the hands of a few of the minister's political friends who sit behind him, and for nothing else. It could not possibly be for anything else, for the road can not possibly pay. And as to the other two small branches that have been tacked on to the Intercolonial, with the effect of increasing the capital cost of that line, this same request had been made to my hon. friend the former Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) and refused by him time and again. Talk about economy! When hon. gentlemen opposite were in Opposition, they were never weary of talking about the extravagance of expending $78,000,000 for the Dominion in one year, that being the highest expenditure under the Liberal Government. The Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), then leader of the Opposition stated time and again that the mere fact that the Government of that day were spending $78,000,000 was prima facie evidence of extravagance and corruption. In two years under the " economy " of which the minister talks, the expenditure was increased something like fifty per cent. But, because they have cut down the expenditure to $25,000,000 less than the terrible extravagance before the beginning of the war, he would have us believe that this is a very economical Government. I think he will have a good deal of trouble in making the

people believe that the Government is an economical one, or to conceal from them the fact that a great deal pf the present expenditure is absolutely without justification.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As to our expenditure on ordinary and capital account being fifty peT cent larger than when we came into office, in the first place the statement is not correct; and, in the second place, I would point out to my hon. friend (Mr. Turriff), that which he always overlooks, that, while in 1911 the total trade of the Dominion was about $800,000,000 in two years it rose to $1,200,000,000, and now it is over $2,000,000,000. This, of course, increases very *greatly the work which must be carried on in administering the affairs of the country. I do not think it desirable or necessary to deal with what the hon. member has said with regard to the Quebec and Saguenay railway. I did not suggest that hon. gentlemen opposite were responsible for the measure that was passed last year, but I cited the fact that they subsidized the railway as showing that they were interested in the completion of a road in that district. It was pointed out last year that the roadbed was falling'away and the wastage in connection with it would have amounted to a great deal in terms of money if the Government had not taken over the road. As to paying Sir Rodolphe Forget $8,000,000, my hon. friend knows that statement is not correct
I said that the total cost to the Government would be in the vicinity of $8,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That statement is not correct. The Government is buying the railway, roadjbed and rails and whatever money the Government pays for that railway in expropriation proceedings will have to go to the parties entitled to it according to law. The statement that the Government is giving $8,000,000 to an individual is absolutely incorrect.

I do not wish to discuss the Quebec and Saguenay now. It will come up in time and then I will discuss it very thoroughly. As with scores of other railways, the late Government granted a subsidy under the statute to a company for the building of that road. Although it was approached several times, the Government never contemplated purchasing the road, and When it failed to be a success and went to pieces because there was no traffic on it, it was not necessarily incumbent upon the Government to come to the rescue, as it
was not a Government railway. However, I do not want to go into details, but I will discuss it very plainly from my point of view when the question comes up. In times of peace it would be altogether wrong to invest in it and in time of war it is an outrage.
On resolution 3:
That the tax shall he paid each year within one month from the date of the mailing of the notice of assessment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a necessary provision. Under the Act as passed last year the assessment can be made up to the first of September and the payment is due on or before the first of November. There is a provision in the Act under'which the time for making the assessment may he extended by the minister, and that has been done frequently, tout there is no provision for extending it from November. Many assessments for the previous year are necessarily made after November because it is not possible to get the information earlier. The result is that the Act is inoperative. As far as the date for payment of the tax is concerned, it is felt that it will make the situation more flexible and more in the interest of the tax-paying community that a period of one month shall be allowed for payment.

If the United States Government carry out the proposal to put a war tax on all imports, that will naturally apply to the wheat which was made free a little while ago by the Government and the farmer will be in a good deal worse position than he was before, because 10 per cent on $2 wheat is twenty cents a bushel and on $1.50 wheat, and that is the lowest it will probably be for a year or more, will be 15 cents a bushel. Wheat previously paid a duty of only ten cents a bushel when entering the United States. I would like to ask if the Government has any intention of doing anything to counterbalance that duty on wheat going into the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not understand my hon. friend when he says "counterbalance." What does my hon. friend mean by that?

The United States purpose putting a ten per cent duty on all imports. On wheat, that my hon. friend made free, there would be a duty of ten per cent going into the United States. It used to cost ten cents a bushel to get wheat into the United States, while, if they put this duty of ten per cent on, it will cost 15 cents,

20 cents or 25 cents a bushel, and I was asking my hon. friend if the Government proposed to do anything to counteract it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know what my hon. friend means by "counterbalance" or "counteract." Does he mean: Arp we going to put duties on wheat and flour on this side to counteract it?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do,not understand it then.
On resolution 4:	'
That with respect to every business liable to taxation hereunder the period for which the returns shall be made and during which it shall be liable for assessment shall be at least thirty-six months, commencing with the beginning of the first accounting period ending after the thirty-first day of December, 1914, or for such less period as the business may have been carried on from the beginning of the said accounting period to the end of the period for which the said tax may be levied under the said Act.
Will the minister explain the latter part of that clause, "or for such less period," etc.?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Firms that have started business since December 31, 1914, would be liable for the three years provided for in the first part of this section if the last part were not added.
If they started business since that time you do not expect to assess them for the full three years, but you expect their assessment to cease at the same time that the other ceases?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, that is right, and therefore they would not be liable for three full years.
Their assessment would commence in May, 1916?
No, from the year they commence business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, for their accounting period. The reason we find it necessary to put in section 4 is that a company might shorten its last accounting period in order to avoid this tax. Although in business for the last five years, they might not be liable to assessment for the full three years unless we in-
9 p.m. serted this section. They might shorten their last accounting period from a year to six or ten months, and the purpose of putting in this section is to safeguard that.

The minister stated that this excess profits tax ceases on the 31st of this calendar year. It has been stated, and I think quite correctly, that the effect of this tax proposed in the resolution has been to discourage the investment of capital in Canada, particularly capital from the United States. That statement has been made by several hon. gentlemen, and to my personal knowledge it is correct. I know of one or two instances in which intended investments have been abandoned. If the minister's statement is correct, might it not be wise to amend the resolution by providing that the tax shall not apply to business commenced this year, or from May, 1917, or perhaps from Alay, 1916, or to capital investment made since that date? It might possibly encourage intended investors to proceed, provided they were assured that they were to be relieved, not from the original 25 per cent tax, but from the taxation under this resolution. The taxation provided for under the resolution is payable in 1918, and it is to be hoped that that year will see the end of the war. I make this suggestion, not with confidence that it is absolutely wise, but in the belief that it is worth considering, and that it will encourage capital investment* and lose nothing to the revenue of the country.
Sir THOMAS.WHITE:	I believe there
are some cases in which extensions were about to be made and the work was interrupted on account of aDnrehension as to the effect of this business profits war taxation; but there was a misunderstanding which, I think, has recently been removed. I have made it clear in the budget speech that this taxation applies only to the last accounting period, the third term provided for in the legislation of last year. I do not think it is necessary to insert a provision such as my hon. friend has in mind for this reason, as I think that has become pretty well known. But, apart from that the liability to taxation under this Act, including of course this amendment which we are considering now, comes to an end on the 31st of December, 1917, by section 21 of the Business Profits War Tax Act which reads:
The provisions of section 3 of this Act shall not continue in force after the 31st of December, 1917.
In other words, we are not extending the term of this Act, and the result is that by the next session of Parliament-that is if it is held after the term of this year-the

operative part of this Act, the taxation section, will have ceased and been determined; and the only operative part of the Act will be that which authorizes the assessment and permits payment in the next year. The reason why I mentioned 1918 in my previous remarks was that I wanted to show that we would have the revenue from this measure in 1918. which we are considering now, and I hoped that that would be a substantial addition to the revenues of the country for that year.

I would like a little information with respect to the administration of the Act. In the settlement of accounts with a company liable to taxation under the Act, is an allowance made for a sinking fund where there is an issue of bonds? Supposing that the trust deed provides for a sinking fund and the company pays the sinking fund to the trustee, is that allowed as a charge against the business?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think my hon. friend will agree that so far as interest, un-on the bonds is concerned that would be a proper expenditure, but in the other case, the redeeming of bonds, to that extent you add to the eauitv of the company in the security; in other words you add -to the capital of the company.

The same thing
would apply to the retirement of. preference shares ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Preference shares are in a different class, because they belong to the proprietor.

I would like to draw
attention to the wording of the last part of clause 4.
[DOT]-shall be at least 36 months, commencing from the beginning of the first accounting period and ending with the 31st day of Decern -' ber, 1918.
Would it not be well to add "and for three accounting periods?" They might not have three accounting periods; they might lengthen their accounting period instead of shortening it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There may be
more than three; they may have one every six months. It is better to have 36 months, as that applies to all in business since the 31st of December, 1914; and then to deal with the case of those who have been in business for less than 36 months, the last part of the section has been inserted.

Does this resolution cover all that the minister is submitting in the Committee of Ways and Means? Does he expect to move the House into Committee of Ways and Means in reference to any further tariff proposals, or in respect to assisting the construction of ships in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not my intention to bring down, any further tariff proposals at this session. Any policy that the Government may determine upon in connection with shipbuilding can be dealt with without taking up the matter in Committee of Ways and Means. It can he done either by legislation or, if we have power under the War Measures Act, by Order in Council.

In connection with
the matter of shipping, a number of the ministers have said that any one desirous of building ships in Canada could have all the orders they could handle by applying to the Imperial Munitions Board, which was acting in conjunction with and for the British Government. I should like to have it clear whether contracts for ships given by the Imperial Munitions Board are financed by the Canadian Government, or whether the Imperial Munitions Board is dealing altogether with Imperial funds.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Board is an Imperial Board, that is to say, the Government of Canada has no control over its operations. It expends the money of the Imperial Government, and not the money of this Government. If I allowed the matter to rest there, the House would not be in possession of full information. The Imperial Government is interested in the matter of shipping, as, indeed,this and every other Government in the world is to-day, on account of the scarcity of ocean tonnage. The Imperial Munitions Board has, I believe, placed orders for some twenty or twenty-two steel ships in Canada of a total tonnage of 160,000 or more. I am speaking from memory. The result is, so far as I know, that by reason of these orders and the orders given by private enterprise in Canada, the ship-building yards of Canada are full to capacity at the present time; in fact I understand they have orders which will keep them busy until about the middle of 1918. The Imperial Government sent over a representative, Mr. Perry, to work in connection with the Imperial Munitions Board. His mission was to inquire into the possibilities of wooden ship-building in

Canada; that is to say, the building of wooden ships which would be suitable for the purposes of the British Government. As the Minister of Marine and Fisheries pointed out the other night, a certain design of wooden ship had been determined upon as being the proper kind of vessel for the purposes of the British Government. I have been interested in this question of shipbuilding, and when it was brought to my attention that the question of finance lay to some extent at the bottom of activities of the British Government in Canada in the matter of shipbuilding, it occurred to me that we could be of assistance. My bon. friend a little while ago spoke slightingly of exchange.

Not at all; rather
laudatory.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
