speechtext: Let me tell my bon. friend that there is more in exchange than was ever dreamed of in his or in my philosophy. I think I can say, without getting my own head or any one else's in the clouds, that the British Government can buy nothing on this continent, on account of exchange conditions, unless they get the credits or the money with which to buy it. In other words, they cannot raise the money by selling in London exchange on America, because exchange has broken down. It occurred to me that the Government of Canada could be of real service to the Imperial Government in connection with its wooden shipbuilding programme in Canada and at the same time do Canada a good turn as well, because it is much to the advantage of Canada to have these wooden ships built here. So I offered the Imperial Munitions Board a credit of $10,000,000 to be availed of as required for the purpose of their shipbuilding programme. That money is to be lent by the Dominion Government to the Imperial Government. When lent to the Imperial Government it will, of course, be money of the Imperial Government -and will constitute a set-off to moneys which the Imperial Government may lend to us in England. In other words, we facilitated the financing of the Imperial Government in connection with its shipbuilding programme in Canada. I received a message from the British Government through the right hon. Mr. Bonar Law, warmly thanking us for our undertaking to finance the British Government in this respect.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce, in dealing with this matter,

certainly left it very far up in the air- about as far up as the exchange problem sometimes goes. But from the explanation made by the Minister of Finance, we know that the Dominion Government is not doing anything in the matter of the construction of ships in Canada, and that the Imperial Government, through the Munitions Board, are having ships built in this country. The Dominion Government, on account of the exchange situation, is simply making an advance of $10,000,000 to the Imperial Government and has no responsibility whatever for the doings of the Imperial Munitions Board in the matter of shipbuilding. The Minister of Trade and Commerce a week ago urged the view that the Government were doing something wonderful in the matter of shipbuilding, but the Minister of Finance and his colleague have made it clear that they are not. As to the assertion that the shipyards in Canada are filled, I have knowledge of the circumstances under which a communication was forwarded to the Imperial Munitions Board some four weeks ago by a certain firm which offered to engage in the construction of wooden ships. Reply was made to the effect that all the contracts for wooden ships had been let. In this shipyard and in others which are in the course of preparation in my province, ships of this kind could be built. The province of Nova Scotia appropriated $2,000,000 for the encouragement of shipbuilding and has appointed a commission for the purpose of arranging for the establishment of shipyards capable of constructing steel and wooden ships. Mr. Norcross, who is head of the Canada Steamship Lines, and who was employed by the Imperial Munitions Board or the Government lately in connection with this matter, in an interview which he gave the public press, urged the absolute necessity of the inauguration by the Dominion Government of a policy of assisting the construction and development of a mercantile marine in Canada-leaving entirely aside the question of the building of small naval vessels.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: After the war, or during the war?

Now. Mr. Norcross is a gentleman who speaks with authority and with some knowledge of the conditions. What I would like to know is whether the Government of Canada intend to take any step towards encouraging the construction of a merchant marine for Canada. The ships to be constructed by the Imperial Munitions Board will, when they leave our shores, not be under Canadian registry;

they will form no part of our transportation system. Lloyd George declared not very long ago that what the Empire needed was ships, and more ships, and more ships. The United States, while working in conjunction with the British Government along lines similar to those being followed by the Imperial Munitions Board, have inaugurated a programme for the construction of wooden and steel ships in order to increase the mercantile marine of the United States, provide means of transportation for the products of that country across the ocean and obviate the difficulty which has arisen through the destruction of vessels by submarines and the consequent depletion of the world's mercantile marine. Having regard to the suggestion of the Prime Minister of Great Britain as to the necessity of obtaining ships, and of the suggestion of Mr. Norcross as to the desirability of the establishment of a Canadian mercantile marine, may I ask whether the Government purposes doing anything by which encouragement will be given to Canadian builders of steel or wooden ships? Is it the ii tention of the Government to take steps to secure the construction of vessels which will form part of a Canadian mercantile marine which will give Canada a means of transportation on the ocean? We have our three transcontinental railway lines to carry our products to the ocean ports, but we have no means of transportation on the sea. The ships to be built by the Imperial Munitions Board are to be placed at the service of the British authorities. This Government should not stand still and do nothing to encourage the construction of ships in Canada which would form part of our ocean transport system and act in co-operation with our system of transportation by land. Will the minister be good enough to tell me the attitude of the Government in regard to the construction of ships in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not agree with my hon. friend that in supplying $10,000,000 of Canada's money for the financing by the Imperial Government of its shipbuilding programme in this country, we are doing nothing. That is a very substantial assistance, and it is so recognized by the Imperial Government. I do not see why my hon. friend should minimize the importance of what we have done. It means that the Imperial Government, which is working in co-operation with our Government in the prosecution of the war and to which it is an object of the utmost
importance to provide transportation in order that the people of the United Kingdom may be fed, has proceeded with a large shipbuilding programme in the Dominion of Canada. Therefore, I submit that the Government should be commended and not adversely criticised for what we have done in assisting to finance the Imperial Government. So far as I am concerned, I am usually indifferent as to whether the Government is praised or not; the main thing is to get the work done whatever it may be, and what has been done is that the Imperial Government has already let contracts to the extent of $10,000,000 for wooden ships of the kind which it requires for the purpose of assisting in the transportation problem.
My hon. friend has raised the further question of establishing a shipbuilding industry in Canada and I am very glad to have the benefit of my hon. friend's views except that they are somewhat vague as indeed are the views of most men on this very important question of shipbuilding. I have been giving the matter, although it does not come immediately under my department, such attention as I have been able, and it is very difficult to determine the course which will produce the best results so far as Canadian transportation is concerned. My hon. friend has pointed out that before the war the railways carried our produce to our ports, and he emphasizes-and I think properly-the question of the importance of ocean transportation; but before the war we had Canadian ships; the railway companies had their shipping lines, and the produce of Canada was moved without difficulty to Great Britain and the continent. At the outbreak of war and since, our mercantile fleet has been to a large extent commandeered by the Imperial Government for the purposes of the prosecution of the war, and, of course, this Government .is not to blame for that. If the Imperial Government desired the shipping belonging to Canadian lines, why, they desired it for the purpose of better prosecuting the war, and so far as I know, no exception can be taken to that course. My hon. friend has raised the question of what should be done to assist the industry of shipbuilding and the transportation problems, present and future. So far as shipbuilding is concerned after the war-and that is, to my mind, an exceedingly important subject, from the standpoint not only of that industry itself, but of the collateral enterprises, such as the steel indus-

try and other industries connected with it -I think a shipbuilding industry cannot be built up in Canada except by bounty legislation. So far as concerns the peace period after the war, if bounty legislation or the granting of subsidies of reasonable amounts would facilitate the creation of a shipbuilding industry in Canada, for my part, I would have no hesitation in saying that I would favour that course. If a shipbuilder were considering the question of establishing a large plant in Canada, I do not think he would be very much bothered as to the question of subsidy during the war, because he would know that every ship that he turned out would sell at a very handsome profit. What he would be concerned about would be the period after the war was over, as to how he would get along during that period when with his plant and fixed charges he would have to meet conditions under which his ships would not sell at the prices they would realize to-day. I have had under consideration the matter of the best plan of assisting the shipbuilding industry, but the matter is not urgent so far as concerns the peri.od immediately following the war, for this reason: I do not believe-and I shall be glad to learn' if I am wrong-that private enterprise can establish a great shipbuilding industry in Canada at this time, because of the shortage of steel plate. I read the other day a statement by Mr. Mark Workman, president of the Dominion Steel Company dealing with that phase of the question and he pointed out-I am speaking from memory and I hope I am not misquoting his statement-that it would be a considerable period before the steel plate would be available for shipbuilding in Canada.
What about building wooden ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have pointed out that the British Government is giving orders for some ten million dollars' worth of wooden ships in Canada, and I may say with regard to wooden ships that while they will serve an emergency purpose, and I think may be useful for coastal business, at the same time the transportation of the future looking to a period considerably beyond the war is bound, I think, to be largely with steel vessels.
Is not the United States building quite a number of wooden ships for transportation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understand the United States is building certain wooden

vessels, but when I was at Washington I learned that the wooden vessel is regarded as an emergency vessel, and it is to steel vessels that transportation interests must-look after the war is over. My hon. friend raises the question whether it would not be advisable for the Dominion Government to consider the establishment of a shipbuilding industry in Canada. Many considerations arise in connection with that, and I think it is a problem which must engage our attention. There is the shortage of steel plate, as my hon. -friend knows, and there is the further question of whether it would be in the interest of the country for the Government to embark in shipbuilding in competition, say, with an enterprise which is ready to take up that industry as soon as it is practicable to do so. For instance, there are in this country some large steel industries which might consider the question, under proper assistance, of establish-ingv a shipbuilding industry. That might be the best way of dealing with the shipbuilding industry, or i-t might be advisable for the Government to consider the establishment of shipbuilding plants, but on account of the difficulty of getting steel plate it is almost impossible to establish a shipbuilding industry in Canada, and, as I have already pointed out, almost every shipbuilding yard in the Dominion, as far as I know, is engaged in the building of steel ships. I would not controvert what my hon. friend says with regard to yards which might build wooden vessels, but I am speaking now of the steel shipbuilding industry. I have taken the matter up with certain of the best posted men in this country, and I find an extraordinary variety and diversity of views as to the best course for the Government to take to assist the shipbuilding industry. I shall have the matter under further consideration and I am endeavouring to ascertain what is the best policy for the Government to pursue.
I can assure my hon. friend that the Dominion Government is anxious to do what it can to promote the shipbuilding industry in this country. When the Government determines upon the policy which it believes will best effectuate that purpose, the necessary announcement will be made to the House, and if legislation is required it will be brought down. That is all I feel disposed to say on the question to-night.
My hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) referred to ships built here being retained on the Canadian register. I am sure he will be interested to know that I raised this very question with the manager of one of

the leading industries in this country. I had iif mind that if the Dominion gave assistance in connection with shipbuilding, one of the conditions might be that the ships so built should remain on the Canadian register and be available for purposes of Canadian transportation. I thought that would be a desirable condition, and I was surprised to learn that in the opinion of this gentleman, who is a very outstanding man in the Canadian industrial world, such a condition would effectually nullify the action of the Dominion Government in giving subsidies and bounties, because he said the shipbuilding industry required to be absolutely free to sell ships, no matter where they were to be used, in order to compete in the markets of the world. It would seem, therefore, that if the ships built in Canada are to remain on the Canadian register they would have to be built and operated by the Dominion Government itself. I do not put forward these suggestions as mature views upon the subject, but as my hon. friend has raised the question I just put these observations forward as representing my state of mind regarding the shipbuilding industry at the present time. If my hon. friend has any suggestions to make of a practical character which will help to solve this problem, and will point out the best way of increasing the transportation facilities of Canada or of building up a great shipbuilding industry in this country, we shall be very glad to hear from him. This question has not escaped the attention of the Government. In the meantime all the shipyards in this country, so far as I know, are engaged in building ships.
When the minister speaks of subsidizing the building of ships, does he refer to ocean tonnage only or to tonnage on inland waters?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was using the
word "subsidies" generally. We should, of course, have to consider the whole situation with regard to subsidizing or giving grants, and I am not prepared to go into details as to the proper policy to-night.

Where are these steel
ships being built at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext:
What about the
White Star?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is the Canadian
White Star and the American White Star. I think I am correct in saying that with the exception of the two Canadian Northern .vessels I have iust mentioned, all the vessels in our transatlantic trade at the outbreak of war were on the British register, and they were nearly all commandeered by the British Government for naval purposes. The Calgarian and the Alsatian of the Allan Line had iust been put on the Atlantic route. They were vessels of the most modern type, and were both commandeered by the British Government. The Calgarian is now doing service as a naval vessel, having been converted into an armed cruiser. I think the same is true of the Alsatian, which is being used somewhere in the east as a flagship for one of the squadrons. I think the_ Empress of Britain was also commandeered for naval purposes. Both the Royal Edward and the Royal George have been used for naval purposes, and one of them was torpedoed and sunk not so very long ago. That was the state of affairs when the war broke out.
I am by no means certain that we shall have the same difficulty in competing with the British shipbuilder after the war. Wages have gone up very much in Great Britain, and I doubt if thev will come down again very rapidly after the war is over. I think even without any form of protection by way of bounty or tariff, our shipbuilders will be able to compete with the

British shipbuilder more easily than before the war. Our shipyards are getting on their feet, so to sneak. Since the formation of the coalition Government by Premier Lloyd George a Department of Shipping has been added to the British Government, and at the head of it is Sir Joseph MacLay, one of the leading shipping men in Great Britain, and a member of one of the leading shipping firms in Glasgow. He has a most intimate knowledge of shipping. I had the opportunity when in England of having many discussions with him and with the members of his staff with regard to this very important question. Hon. gentlemen know of the tremendous shortage in shipping that the British Empire has to face. Many vessels have been torpedoed and many have been mined, and it has been found impossible t;o replace the tonnage from British shipyards as fast as it is destroyed. Great Britain has also been supplying tonnage to our Allies for the transport of troops and munitions. I understand that in connection with the operations at Saloniki alone, several hundred British ships are employed all the time. The result is that there is a great shortage of tonnage for carrying to Great Britain the products from overseas which are so essential not only to the comfort but to the absolute existence of the people of the British Isles at the present time. The Shipping Board under the direction of Sir Joseph MacLay are doing all they can to meet that difficulty. All the shipyards in the United Kingdom are working at high pressure, but many of them are turning out naval vessels entirely. The result is that the merchant shipping which is being turned out is not as great as the shipping which is being destroyed by submarines and mines from week to week. In discussing the matter with Sir Joseph MacLay, I expressed the belief that a considerable amount of work might be done in Canada in building ships to take the place of those that are being lost to Great Britain at the present time.
Are we building any?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
At present ships aTe being built in Canada for the British Government, under the direction of the Department of the Controller of Shipping and under the management of the Imperial Munitions Board which, in Canada, is acting for the Shipping Department of Great Britain. At present the shipyards in Canada are doing a very great deal of work building ships for the British- Government, for British

trade, and for certain other purposes which I cannot mention to the House at this time. This is true of the shipyard at Quebec which is controlled by Mr. George Davie, the shipyard at Montreal belonging to the Canadian Vickers, the shipyard at Collingwoo-d, the Poison yard at Toronto-, the Thor Iron Works of Toronto, the shipyard at Port Arthur, the shipyard of Messrs. Coghlan and the Wallace shipyard in the province of British Columbia, and also the shipyard at New Glasgow, Nova Scotia, of the Nova Scotia Steel Company.
What is the highest tonnage?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
-Ships are being built in
Canada to-day up to 8,000 tons. But, if my information is correct, the Imperial Munitions Board, acting for the Controller of Shipping, is desirous that the ships they shall make contracts for at present shall not be as large as that, but shall be, at the largest, in the neighbourhood of 3,000 tons.
What is the minimum tonnage?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Wooden ships are being
built in Canada for the British Government and -under the Munitions Board. The instructions that the Munitions Board -have from the British Government is, that they shall not enter into -a contract for *wooden ships of less than 2,500 tons. The [DOT]reason for that condition I do not quite understand. I took the opportunity of making representations on the -subject to the Controller of Shipping and also to the Colonial Secretary, Right Hon. Walter Long. I pointed out that there were yards in -Canada that could build wooden ships of a less tonnage than 2,500 tons, but that [DOT]with their equipment and in view of the difficulty of procuring material and finding men to- do the work, it would be impossible in the case of many of them to -build ships as large as 2,500 tons. That is a matter that has to be decided by the British Government and the Controller of Shipping, as -they aTe the ones for whom ships are being -built.
So much for the shipyards that may be called standard or established shipyards, equipped for building steel vessels or equipped for building wooden vessels. There are many other yards in Canada in which wooden- ships could be built. That is particularly true, I think, of the Maritime Provinces. I am told that there are being constructed in Nova Scotia 48 wooden

ships, the largest probably of 1,500 tons and the smallest of 150 tons, or probably less. These are being built by private individuals, and from what I can learn of the conditions to-day, as soon as they are completed their builders will be able to sell them at figures that will be profitable, or, if they operate and manage these ships themselves, at the present rates of freight prevailing in the world, if the ships have the luck to escape being torpedoed or submarined, they will, in a few voyages, earn enough to pay for the entire cost of construction. With the impetus given to the building of ships in Canada by the conditions arising from the war, I believe that after the war is over our shipbuilding yards and shipbuilders will be in a better position to compete with the British shipbuilder than before the war broke out, and this entirely apart from the fact that I believe that conditions will have so changed, so far as cost is concerned, that the competition will be on more equal terms.
Something has been said this evening about the conditions likely to exist after the war. From what I can learn in talking with shipping men on the other side of the water and on this side also, I believe that, even if the war should come to a close during the present year-a matter about which I entertain very grave doubts indeed -the shortage of shipping will be so great that the shipyards in Canada and Great Britain, as well as in other parts of the world, can continue for a good many years turning out ships at their utmost capacity without overtaking what the normal quantity of ships should be and what it was when the war broke out. After the war an immense deal of shipping will be required for many purposes. Suppose, for instance, that Canada has 400,000 troops overseas at the conclusion of the war, it will take a ship a day for a year carrying
1,000	men each to 'bring these soldiers back to Canada. There are troops from Great Britain in all the theatres of the war who will need to be brought across seas. Then transportation must be provided for all the equipment, the guns' and all varied articles necessary in carrying on the war. Besides, many countries are so depleted in stocks of goods essential for the carrying on of successful business and for comfortable conditions of living that after the war there will be an enormous traffic on the seas. I am assured by shipping men, who know far more about these matters than I do, that for a long time after the war is over freights will be very high, not so high as
to-day, perhaps, but high as compared with what they were at the outbreak of the war and high enough to assure to shipowners a good return on their investment. Shipbuilders in Canada are alive to the conditions that exist and expect that the result will1 be the development of shipbuilding in Canada.
I agree with the hon, member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) as to the desirability of having ships registered in Canada. It is most desirable that we should have a large mercantile marine of our own. The position I have taken with regard to commandeering ships is this: as to ships of British register, I have regarded it as quite proper that the British Government should commandeer them for any purpose in connection with the war; but, as to ships of Canadian register, should the British Government require these ships they should ask us for them. An Order in Council to that effect was passed soon after the outbreak of the war, and that is the policy that is being carried into effect to-day.
Do I understand the minister to urge as a matter of policy that Canadian shipbuilders be allowed to dispose of the ships they construct to Canadians only?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Not at all, at the present juncture. I have never urged that, and would not think of putting forward such a proposition. What I did say was that when the British Government requires ships for any purpose in connection with the war, if the vessels are of British register, in my opinion they have the right to commandeer them without regard to us in Canada, even though Canadians may be owners of shares, or even owners of the ships themselves; but if the vessels are of Canadian register, then the British Government, while they may have the legal power, have not the constitutional right, to commandeer those ships, but if they are to be commandeered it should 'be done through the Government of Canada.
That position was adopted by the Government. Soon after the war broke out and before much consideration of the matter, they started commandeering ships of Canadian register. We drew their attention to the matter and put our views clearly before them. They accepted our views in effect. We passed an Order in Council on the subject and now, when Canadian ships are required for naval purposes in connection with the war by the controller of shipping under the British Government, they communicate with usandask us to com-

mandeer those ships and have them placed at their disposal. In connection with the matter very great difficulties arise. We will be informed, for instance, by the British Government that a certain vessel of Canadian register is necessary for the successful carrying on of the war and for the carrying of commodities that are necessary for the life of the British public. We will communicate with the owners of the vessel in Canada where it is registered. We, in many cases, will receive protests from them against the British Government commandeering the vessel, or it will be pointed out that vessel is necessary to Canada, that it may be carrying something that is necessary for the purpose of enabling munitions factories in certain parts to carry out their contracts successfully. From time to time our department is up against questions of that sort that we have to deal with, having on the one hand the desire of every Canadian to win the war and the desire of. every Canadian also to see that Great Britain is not hampered in carrying on the war by getting those products from overseas which are esssential to the people of the Mother Country, and, on the other hand, considering whether any injustice will be done to Canadian interests if we allow the ships to go. These are questions that we are face to face with every day and which cause very great difficulty.
In dealing with that matter and applying our best judgment from the patriotic and practical standpoint, a considerable number of Canadian vessels were commandeered for the service of the Government of Great Britain, and unfortunately a number of these vessels have been torpedoed, as have Canadian vessels that have not been commandeered by the British Government, and the result is that great difficulty exists in obtaining a supply of tonnage sufficient for our own purposes at the present time. There are difficulties in connection with the coalcarrying trade that my hon. friend from Nova Scotia will understand. There is the difficulty of getting sufficient tonnage to bring the coal from the mines of Nova Scotia to the St. Lawrence ports and also to carry it to St. John and Halifax. In some cases that difficulty might be met by railway traffic to a certain extent. There are difficulties also in connection with the oil vessels that are required to bring oil to Canada for the munitions works.

Will the minister say if the Government have commandeered any

vessels under the Order in Council of which he speaks?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes. we have. At the request of the British Government we have commandeered certain Canadian vessels in order that they might be available for helping in the prosecution of the war and in connection with matters that were represented to us by the British Government as being essential, and in some cases vessels vitally necessary, for the prosecution of the war.
The commandeering has not then been for the use of the Canadian Government but of the Admiralty?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
For the use of the Imperial Government to carry on the war. That is the position of the matter to-day. The subject is one of tremendous interest and importance. I have not , yet heard any one in this House suggest that we should pay a bounty for the construction of vessels in Canada. I do not think that is suggested at the present time or that we should, under existing circumstances-if we have the power to do it and I think we have-provide protection by means of a tariff so as to protect us against the ship-builders in Great Britain. There is no need of that at present because practically all the yards where steel ships can be built are busy and in addition, many yards where wooden vessels can be built are busy. In Nova Scotia there are forty-eight wooden ships building.
What we are more concerned with is the auestion as to what the condi-
10 p.m. tion of shipbuilding will be after the war. The matter is deserving of the greatest possible consideration and it is receiving that consideration. Although the war is costing us a tremendous sum of money, and although I know that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has no easy task in financing the war at the present time and has tremendous responsibilities resting upon his shoulders, yet it is a subject worthy of consideration whether or not this country should not build ships to be owned by the Government of Canada and to be operated in connection with Canadian railways across the water even though it will involve a very large expenditure and an expenditure which might be difficult to finance at the present time. These are considerations to which the Government is giving consideration at the present time and I may say that if any hon. gentleman, on this or the other side of the House, has any suggestion to make about the matter, we

will be only too delighted to receive his suggestion and give it our very best consideration.

Mr. Chairman, the matter of shipbuilding in Canada is one of great interest to all who would desire to see the establishment of an industry of this character. As far as wooden shipbuilding in Nova Scotia is concerned, I think it is about in the same position that it was in three or four years ago. I would assume that in normal times about the number of wooden ships mentioned by my -hon. friend the Minister of Marine (Mr. Hazen) are under construction as are being built today.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Forty-eight.

The minister
states that there are only forty-eight new ships under construction in Nova Scotia and I would say that in normal times there would be nearly that number under construction. I would hardly say that he was correctly advised in saying that there were ships being built of 1,500 tons. I would imagine that the largest tonnage would be somewhere in the vicinity of 500 or 600 tons. There are a great many obstacles in the way of building ships of from 1,500 to 2,500 tons in the Maritime Provinces. I doubt if it would be practicable anywhere in the Maritime Provinces. It would be very difficult to obtain timber suitable for the construction of vessels of that size. The minister stated that it was the policy of the British Government to construct wooden ships of 2,500 tons. I think that is an unfortunate policy to adopt and I am very glad that the minister saw fit to question the propriety of a policy of that kind in England. It may be possible to build wooden ships of that size on the Pacific coast but I doubt very much if it is possible to build them in the Maritime Provinces. I speak with some hesitancy in this respect because possibly I may be in error, but I doubt very much if the wood is available. There is also the question of the difficulty of obtaining labour in the Maritime Provinces. It is at the present moment extremely difficult for shipbuilders to obtain anything like the quantity of labour required. This has been aggravated recently by visits to Nova Scotia ports by representatives of American shipbuilding yards to secure labour. I received a letter only to-day from an acquaintance of mine who is engaged in shipbuilding protesting against the fact that representatives of -shipbuilding yards 106
in the state of Maine have recently -been in Nova -Scotia and have been offering wages of from $6 to $12 a day. He asked me to protest to the Government against the invasion of our labour market by people from the United States. My correspondent insisted that this be prevented just as the Dominion Government were asked to refrain from encouraging immigration from the United States into -Canada. Probably thi-s will soon pass away, because I think you will find that the wooden shipbuilding programme outlined recently by the United States is an impossible one, especially on anything like the scale contemplated.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They have got down now to 250; it was 1,000 before.

I do not imagine that they can build even 250. If the British Government are anxious to have wooden ships constructed in Canada their policy should be a practical one, and the tonnage of such vessels should 'be within the capabilities of Canadian shi-p builders. I quite agree with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in respect to steel shipbuilding in the future. Prior to the war I doubt if anybody could have said that shipbuilding was a practical industry to be contemplated in this country'for a great number of years to come, unless very substantial assistance was granted -by the Government by way of bounty toward that end, and that policy would be a very doubtful one, indeed, for Canada to embark upon. I think the situation has changed entirely. As the minister has said, it is recognized in England that production costs in that country for the future will be greatly in excess of what they were prior to the war. The wages paid to labour for British -shipyards will 'be much greater, probably, than they were in the days prior to the war. Shipbuilding labour was not as strongly organized in Great Britain as was other labour, but, having once become accustomed to a few years of higher wages, the shipbuilding labourers are not likely to permit their wages to fall. That is the history of wages in all countries, namely, when once they have risen from a low rate they -are not likely to fall back again. So it is generally expected that the cost of producing -ships in Great Britain will be much higher in the future than it has been in the past. If we wish to make a start in the construction of steel ships in Canada this is the opportune moment. I doubt if it is a practical way of dealing with the matter to say that -some time after the war we may consider the policy of subsidizing shipbuilding.



I think the subsidizing of shipbuilding by bounty is a very doubtful policy, indeed, and I doubt very much if we should at the present moment commit ourselves to it. At [DOT] any rate, it is not necessary' to pay a bounty to-day to shipbuilders in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Hear, hear.

They are not asking for it, and they do not deserve it. The obstacles to-day confronting shipbuilders are the cost of purchasing the plant and equipment, and, in fact, the difficulty of obtaining a plant at all. There is a further difficulty in obtaining plates. These obstacles render it almost impossible for private capital to engage in any extensive shipbuilding programme, and it has been suggested-I have heard it discussed by prominent shipbuilders in the United States, and by some Canadians-that if the Governments of this country, provincial or federal, desired to aid shipbuilding, they should do something in the way of advancing capital to competent persons to start shipbuilding yards. A shipbuilding plant costs 100 per cent more to-day than it would in normal times, and the cost of plate is also excessive. Therefore private enterprise could hardly be expected to engage in the commencement of a shipbuilding industry in these circumstances. In respect to the securing of plate, I was advised recently that the Imperial Munitions Board or the Canadian Government had made some arrangement with the United States Government whereby some of the steel plants in the United States would supply Canadian yards with all the shipbuilding plate required for the next two or three years. There may have been no such arrangement made, but if not I think it is an arrangement which very well might be made. I think the United States Government would be quite willing, if requested so to do by the Canadian Government, to make arrangements whereby some of their plants would be at the disposal of Canadian ship. building yards for the purpose of supplying plate. It would not be a very large quantity anyway. If there has been no such arrangement made, and there is any demand on behalf of Canadian shipbuilding yards for plate, I think this matter might very well be taken up. I agree with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) that this is the opportunity for Canadians to commence steel shipbuilding. If they do not do so now, they are not likely to do so for a great number of years. If a company were ready to construct ships to-day,
f.\Ir. A. K. Maclean.]
I think beyond doubt they could readily secure contracts which would keep them going for "five or ten years.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Hear, hear.

And by that time they might be able to liquidate their capt-tal investment almost entirely, so that long after the war had ended and the demand for shipping had been pretty well supplied, these companies might he able to carry on their business without a subsidy. In substance, what I have to suggest as a proper policy is this: that companies, if properly organized by men who have had experience and are willing to contribute some capital, be assisted in some way by the Government. I do not intend to suggest details of the arrangement; I prefer to simply state it in general terms. I think it would have been better for the British Government to have assisted Canadian yards in this matter in preference to asking Canadian shipbuilding yards to construct wooden ships of 2,500 tons. I think it is quite possible to equip steel shipbuilding plants and turn out 100,000 tons of shipping in a year, and it is quite possible to equip yards for that purpose inside of six months. And if a few shipyards of that capacity were started, the total tonnage they could supply in the next two or three years would be very considerable.

It is my duty to point out that rule 13 of this House provides:
Speeches in Committee of the Whole must he strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
I think the reading of the rule will be quite sufficient.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that two or three weeks ago I ventured to make a suggestion in regard to this matter, I feel disposed to trespass on your time for two or three minutes tonight. I said then that I should like to see this Government or any Government in Canada take from the public treasury of this country $10,000,000 or $15,000,000 if necessary to build ships to carry Canadian flour-I specified that as one article -from Canadian ports free across the ocean. From what has been said in the discussion here to-night, I am more than ever confirmed in my opinion that the Government would be justified in taking that course. Both parties have endeavoured to benefit the whole of Canada by building lines of

railway. It was felt that the Canadian Pacific Railway was not sufficient, that the building of another line would result in competition which would give the lowest possible rates. I believe that our railway lines can compete with those of the United States in the matter of rates for the carrying of grain from the West to ocean ports. Why is it, then, that 60 per cent or more of our grain finds its way over American railway lines to American ports on its way ' across the ocean? The reason is simply that tonnage is more readily found at Boston and New York than at Halifax, Mont-, real and St. John. That condition will be accentuated after the war is over if no steps are taken to remedy it. The time is now opportune for the Canadian Government to embark on a scheme for building ships. We need not be deterred from taking that course because of the existence of privately owned shipyards. There could not be a better time for starting than the present, because the loss of tonnage has been so great that for many years the privately-owned yards will have more than they can do. If we are justified in taking from the public treasury money to build Government lines of railroad for the transportation of produce we are justified also in taking money from the treasury to establish transportation lines across the ocean. Moreover, I believe that the produce of Canada is discriminated against by the carrying of our wheat and flour across the ocean in vessels which represent the investment of British capital. Why should it cost three or four times as much to carry 100 pounds of flour across the ocean as it does to carry 100 pounds of wheat? I believe it is because many of the British millers, who have invested their money in vessels that are carrying our wheat across the ocean, place a high rate on flour in order to discourage the manufacture of flour in Canada and to have wheat carried across for their mills. That is a circumstance which justifies Government action. I need not point out the great advantage it would be to the whole Dominion if the Government would embark on a scheme of building ships to carry flour across the ocean free. Inducement would be held out for the carrying of our wheat over Canadian lines and there would be a corresponding benefit to our Canadian railways. Two of our transcontinental lines are finding it hard to get' along.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend have only wheat carried free, or would he have everything the country produces-lumber, cheese and so on-carried free?
106}	]j |

No, I would have flour carried free, but not wheat. Wheat, however, which had been carried over Canadian lines to Canadian ports,- should be transported at as low a rate as possible; I would suggest that the rate be such as to hold out an inducement for the manufacture of the wheat into flour in Canada. The advantage which would result to the stock raisers and farmers of Canada is obvious. I do not think that lumber or cheese are in the same category as wheat. Reasons might be advanced why other produce might be carried free, but they do not occur to me. This scheme would be an advantage to the stock raisers and farmers generally in Ontario, Quebec and the Maritime Provinces. It would be an advantage to the farmers of the West, for they would obtain, a few cents a bushel more for their wheat. It would be an advantage to the three transcontinental railway lines and to the-men employed ,on them. The advantage-resulting from the impetus to the shipbuilding industry would be more than it is possible to express in words. There will be-a great shortage in tonnage after the war is over and unless a bold and vigorous policy is followed in the matter of building ships and providing shipping we shall have to depend on other more progressive countries for the transportation of our produce across the ocean. I merely wish to emphasize what I said on a former occasion : that I will endorse the policy advanced by any party of taking from the public treasury sufficient money to build Canadian ships under the supervision and control of the Dominion Government.

I am sorry that I did not hear what the Finance Minister said on this subject, in which everybody is so deeply interested. In listening to the discussion, I was surprised to have the idea forced upon my mind that the Government is still without a shipbuilding policy. We had a discussion a few evenings ago on this subject, and on that occasion the Minister of Trade and Commerce informed us that everything was being done; that the Government had adopted a shipbuilding policy; that it was in operation and working splendidly. It appears, however, that hon. gentlemen opposite are still at sea on this important auestion; that they have no policy in the matter. I am sorry for this, because it is a matter of vital importance to the people that a definite policy of shipbuilding should be inaugurated. We have an example of that in t(he proposal

made by my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) who suggests that the Government should build ships to carry flour free across the Atlantic. I must enter a Drotest against that proposal. I cannot distinguish between flour and other commodities that we have for sale in so far as they would be affected by my hon. friend's proposal. I see no reason why flour should be carried free. Indeed, I am told that you can buy Canadian flour cheaper in Liverpool than you can in Montreal or Winnipeg. If that is true, it would be more advisable for my hon. friend to advocate that vessels be built to carry flour across from England free, so that Canada could get flour more cheaply. But that is a question which I think we do not need to discuss. I have not a policy ready but I have no doubt that the shipbuilding people of this country would be glad to consult with the minister in regard to this matter if he would call them together. Let me suggest to him that he announce that he is ready to do something in the way of stimulating this industry in Canada and that he is willing to meet the people throughout the country who are interested in shipbuilding, and I venture to say that he will have them call on him readily and give him their views. This I have no doubt will be of some value to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have met many of them and I have received many different suggestions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: So have I.
Are we to hope that any of these suggestions are to be put in force or will they go in at one ear and out at the other and nothing be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend is a man
interested in shipping and perhaps he will give us some suggestions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He started out to do so.

As I have stated on
many occasions, all articles entering into the construction of ships should be admitted free of duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They are nearly all admitted free now.
I beg my hon. friend's pardon. There are scores of things that enter into the construction of ships that are heavily taxed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend will pardon me. He will find that the plates, the knees,

the machinery, nearly everything that enters into the construction of a steel ship is either admitted free, or entitled to a drawback pf 99 per cent. .
Everything?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Practically everything.
Everything that is imported.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

That would not be
necessary on what is not imported.
I can mention scores of things that are manufactured in Canada and that enter into the construction of ships and that are heavily taxed, and there is no drawback.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is no taxation on the plates.	*

My hon. friend can
easily turn up the tariff and read a list of things that enter into the construction of ships and which, are taxed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have never yet met a
shipbuilder who thinks that the admittance of such articles free would encourage shipbuilding to any extent. It is a mere drop in the bucket.
I have never met a shipbuilder who did not hold a view contrary to that expressed by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: You must have met different ones from those I have met.

You can allow these
articles that enter into the construction of a ship to enter this country free of duty so that the shipbuilder will have an opportunity of securing cheap material, because at present he cannot successfully compete with the shipbuilder on the other side of the water where the articles do enter free of duty.' A large quantity of paint, for example, is used in the shipbuilding trade. In England, if a shipbuilder wants to buy paint he buys the paint in the cheapest market in the world. A shipbuilder cannot get paint in Canada at the same rate as he could in the old country; he has Ito pay a high duty. If paint is manufactured here, the manufacturer sees that the consumer pays the duty; if it is impbrted, the duty is paid at the customs house. That is only one example. '

Following out your suggestion, why not build the ships somewhere else entirely? You would argue that the

ships should be built in England or in the United States or anywhere else where they could be built at the cheapest rate.

We shall never be able to build ships in Canada unless we build them as cheaply as they can be built elsewhere or unless the Government will make up the difference in .the cost. When a ship is built, it has to compete with all the world for business.
If there is a cargo to be carried, that cargo is set up at auction by the brokers in London and the man who gives the lowest bid will get the cargo. If it is a cargo of grain to be carried from the River Plate, to Liverpool, the man who will carry it for one cent per hundred pounds less than the Canadian will get it, and if the Canadian ship costs $10, or $15 a ton more to build than the ship built on the Clyde, the Canadian in ordinary times can not earn the interest on his investment. That is the experience in the past and it will be the experience in the future. This is a vital question. If you give the Canadian builder an opportunity, he will be able to compete with the world. Free material is one of the things he must have if he is going to get along at all. It is a question for the Government to consider as to how that can best be done. The raw material which enters into the building of the ships costs jnore in Canada than in the Old Country.
How about wages?

That question has also to be considered. The Government must solve the problem of how the difference in cost is to be made up, if they are going to help out the shipbuilding industry. My hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) has said that he has met many people and that they have given him suggestions. What I would like to see is that he should put some of those suggestions into practice and give us his policy. The fact that freights are high at present and that everything is abnormal does not relieve him from the necessity of doing something. This is the time to prepare for the competition in shipbuilding that is bound to come as soon as the war is over, and the sooner that he sets about doing something, the better. I trust that something	will grow out of this
discussion.	We have already had many
discussions- on this subject, but they have all ended in the same way, that is, there has been no results from all that has been said. I am glad to know that my hon. friend has
adopted the suggestion that I have made to him several times in regard to the commandeering of Canadian ships. Shortly after the war broke out, I brought this matter up in the House, and I took the ground that if ships on the Canadian register were to be commandeered, the commandeering should be done by the Canadian Government. That was not done at the first; it was not done in the year 1915, although I had brought the matter to the attention of the Government on several occasions. I am very much pleased, however, to know that the Government has arrived at that decision, because it is the proper decision: that if Canadian ships are to be used in the war by the Imperial Government, if they are on the Canadian register, they ought to be commandeered by the Canadian Government. In this matter the Government have taken a step in the right direction, and I wish to express my approval. If they will examine into the question they will find it is impossible in normal times for a Canadian shipbuilder to compete with the builder on the other .side under present conditions. Let us hope that the minister will call together the shipbuilders from the different districts in Canada where they are engaged in this industry, and see what can be done in order to stimulate the industry and in order to start it in places where it has not been started so far. The minister knows very well the difficulty of getting material at the present time. It is almost out of the question to build any large number of steel ships at present, because you cannot secure the material with which to build them. I do not know what the minister's plan is in regard to wooden ships; if it is to build wooden ships with steel frames and wooden planks, I suppose we could do that successfully in eastern Canada. I do not know what the plan is, and I do not think that the offers that have been made by the Imperial Munitions Board are going to help the shipbuilders very much, because, so far as I can learn, they are not as good as the terms that can be obtained from ordinary merchants who want ships for ordinary trade. I am told that the proposal of the Imperial Munitions Board is to give a small percentage of profit to the builder; that the builder who invests his capital in the enterprise and produces the ships will have them purchased from him by the Imperial Munitions Board and a small amount such as eight or ten per cent will be given him as a profit

for building. The ordinary shipbuilder who
. has the ordinary common business ability that these people 'have can make a much better profit by dealing with some merchant who requires a ship.
There is nothing in the proposals of the Munitions Board, so far as I can learn, to stimulate shipbuilding very much in Canada. The fact that freights are high has done something, of course, to stimulate the industry. It is up to the Government to deal with this question themselves, and not leave it to the Munitions Board. Some policy should be framed by the Government without delay, which will establish the shipping industry in places where it does not already exist, and develop it in places where it has already been started.
Does the Minister of Marine and Fisheries know where the plates are being obtained for these steel ships?
